META.subject: Chemistry
META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 3.1 (10 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Chemistry
UNIT.content:
• Simple classification of substances as either acids or bases
• Definition of acids and bases (Arrhenius Definition)
• Chemical properties of acids and bases
• Strength of acids and bases (pH scale, strong and weak acids and bases)
• Uses of acids and bases
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) classify substances as either acids or bases using indicators in the laboratory and in everyday life
b) define acids and bases using the Arrhenius definition
c) investigate the chemical properties of acids and bases, including their reactions with metals, carbonates and each other (neutralisation)
d) determine the strength of acids and bases using the pH scale and universal indicator, and distinguish strong from weak acids and bases
e) appreciate the uses of acids and bases in day-to-day life, including safe handling and the use of antacids to relieve hyperacidity
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Critical thinking and problem solving: learners interpret pH data for household products and hypothesise why each is acidic or basic
• Communication and collaboration: learners discuss findings in groups, cold-call responses, and present models and explanations
• Self-efficacy: learners carry out indicator tests and neutralisation investigations and gain confidence in laboratory work
• Digital literacy: learners interpret graphs and use simulations of pH where available
• Learning to learn: learners track their questions on the Driving Question Board and revise their models as evidence grows
UNIT.values:
• Responsibility: handling acids, bases and household chemicals safely and disposing of them properly
• Integrity: reporting observations honestly, even when they differ from predictions
• Unity: working cooperatively in practical groups
• Respect: caring for shared apparatus and for classmates' ideas
UNIT.sep:
• Asking questions and defining problems: learners generate questions about why products differ in pH and add them to the DQB
• Analyzing and interpreting data: learners read the pH graph of household products and classify them
• Planning and carrying out investigations: learners test local materials with indicators such as red cabbage extract, litmus and universal indicator
• Developing and using models: learners build and revise particle models of H⁺ and OH⁻ ions in solution
• Constructing explanations: learners explain why antacids relieve hyperacidity using neutralisation
• Engaging in argument from evidence: learners argue whether alkalinity determines a substance's use
UNIT.pcis:
• Health education: safe use of antacids, avoiding misuse of household chemicals and understanding hyperacidity and ulcers
• Safety and security: laboratory safety rules, hazard labels and storage of corrosive substances at home
• Environmental education: effects of acidic and basic waste, acid rain and soil acidity on the environment
• Life skills: making informed decisions on the use of cleaning and food products
UNIT.careers:
• Pharmacist: formulates and dispenses antacids such as magnesium hydroxide and aluminium hydroxide
• Agronomist/farmer: tests soil pH in Kericho tea farms and Rift Valley maize farms and applies lime to correct acidity
• Food technologist: uses acids such as citric and ethanoic acid to preserve and flavour foods
• Water and environmental analyst: monitors pH of Lake Victoria and industrial effluent
• Medical doctor/clinical officer: treats hyperacidity, gastritis and ulcers
UNIT.focus: This unit uses a graph of the pH values of everyday Kenyan household products to anchor learning about acids and bases. Learners predict, test, explain and model how the properties of acids and bases, their strength and their ionic nature determine their uses and safety precautions. Through investigations, learners build towards explaining why alkaline antacids are given to patients with hyperacidity.
UNIT.phenomenon: The teacher displays a set of household products found in many Kenyan homes: lemon juice (from Kisumu market), baking soda (used for mandazi), bar soap, and vinegar. A graph shows the pH value of each product: lemon juice and vinegar have low pH values, while baking soda and soap have higher pH values above 7. Learners must interpret the data and hypothesise why each product is acidic or basic. It is puzzling because the products look similar (clear or white and found in the same kitchen), yet the lemon juice tastes sour and the soap feels slippery. Some are safe to eat, such as lemon juice and vinegar, while others, such as soap, are harmful if swallowed, and these properties influence how each product is used and what safety precautions are needed. Learners discuss how these properties relate to everyday uses, such as vinegar for pickling and soap for cleaning.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• A person with heartburn after eating a heavy meal of nyama choma and fried foods takes an antacid tablet and feels relief
• Tea farmers in Kericho add lime to acidic soil to improve crop yields
• Lemon juice rubbed on a rusted or tarnished metal surface cleans it, but soap does not
• Red cabbage extract changes colour when mixed with lemon juice, soap solution and baking soda
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: Does the alkalinity of a substance determine its uses in day to day life? Why are patients with hyperacidity issues given antacid medications?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. How do we classify substances as acids or bases?
2. Why are acids and bases important in our day-to-day life?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: Phenomenon – Students examine the pH graph of lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda and soap, predict why each is acidic or basic, and raise questions for the Driving Question Board.
Lesson 2: Simple classification – Students test household substances with litmus and red cabbage extract and sort them as acids or bases.
Lesson 3: Natural and laboratory indicators – Students compare indicator colour changes, build a classification table and revise their initial hypotheses.
Lesson 4: Arrhenius definition (acids) – Students use models and simulations to show that acids produce H⁺ ions in water and explain why lemon juice is sour.
Lesson 5: Arrhenius definition (bases) – Students show that bases and alkalis produce OH⁻ ions in water, explain why soap feels slippery, and update their particle models.
Lesson 6: Chemical properties I – Students investigate reactions of acids with metals and carbonates, such as vinegar with baking soda, and identify the gases produced.
Lesson 7: Chemical properties II – Students investigate neutralisation between acids and bases and link it to how antacids relieve hyperacidity.
Lesson 8: Strength of acids and bases – Students use universal indicator and the pH scale to compare strong and weak acids and bases, and relate strength to ion concentration.
Lesson 9: Uses of acids and bases – Students analyse uses in food preservation, cleaning, farming (lime for acidic soil) and medicine, and evaluate safety precautions.
Lesson 10: Consolidation – Students complete their final models, answer the driving question about alkalinity and antacids, and present claims using evidence from the unit.

LESSONS.title: Phenomenon: Why Do Lemon Juice, Vinegar, Baking Soda and Soap Behave So Differently?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: acid, base, alkali, pH, pH scale, neutral, sour, slippery, hypothesis, hyperacidity, antacid, Driving Question Board

slo.purpose: To launch the unit by confronting learners with the puzzling phenomenon that four similar-looking household products differ sharply in taste, feel, pH and safety, and to open the Driving Question Board (DQB).
slo.knowledge: Learners interpret the pH graph to see that lemon juice (pH 2.0) and vinegar (pH 2.8) fall below 7, while baking soda solution (pH 8.3) and soap solution (pH 10.0) fall above 7, with pure water (pH 7.0) as the reference. They link sour and slippery observations to these values and to how the products are used.
slo.skills: Interpreting data from a graph (SEP 4: Analysing and Interpreting Data); asking questions (SEP 1); making predictions and generating hypotheses; communicating ideas in pairs and as a class.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about everyday substances, respect for peers' ideas, and a safety-conscious attitude: never taste or touch unknown chemicals in the laboratory or at home.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we classify substances as acids or bases? 2. Why are acids and bases important in our day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 launches the phenomenon and the DQB. Learners notice that the products fall on either side of 7 and propose initial ideas and questions. These ideas are revisited in Lessons 2-3, where learners classify the same products using indicators, and they seed the particle model that is revised in every later lesson. Learners are not told WHY the products differ; that is built across the unit.
slo.safetyNotes: The products are displayed only for looking. Nobody tastes lab chemicals. Learners must not taste the products in class; sour and slippery observations are given as reported data (lemon juice and vinegar are safe in food, baking soda is safe in small amounts in food, and soap is harmful if swallowed). Learners may touch the soap solution only if the teacher allows it, then wash their hands. Use clean, labelled containers and keep soap solution away from eyes.

LESSONS.overview: Mrs Achieng's class in Kisumu sees four products on the front bench: lemon juice bought from Kisumu market, vinegar used by mama mboga for pickling kachumbari, baking soda used by Mama Wanjiru for mandazi, and a bar of soap. In clear cups they all look similar. Yet Otieno asks why lemon is sour, and Wanjiru asks why soap is slippery. Learners predict how the products differ, study a pH graph (lemon juice 2.0, vinegar 2.8, pure water 7.0, baking soda 8.3, soap 10.0), build hypotheses, and raise questions for the DQB. The driving question is: Does the alkalinity of a substance determine its uses in day to day life? Why are patients with hyperacidity issues given antacid medications? They draw an initial particle model, which will be revised in every lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the four products displayed in clear cups on the teacher's bench: lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda solution and soap solution. In pairs (3 minutes) they answer in their notebooks: (a) Which products do you think are safe to eat and which are harmful? (b) Which are alike and which are different? (c) Predict how the pH values would be arranged on a scale from 0 to 14 for these products. They write a quick prediction and a reason, using what they know from the kitchen at home, for example lemon in tea, vinegar on kachumbari, and soap for washing clothes.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the products before learners enter, with labels. Say: 'These four things sit in many Kenyan kitchens. Look at them carefully. Do not taste or touch them.' Ask: 'Without any equipment, how could we tell them apart?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before taking answers. Cold-call 4 learners for their predictions and record them on the board under 'Our first ideas' without judging as right or wrong. Then ask: 'Otieno says lemon juice is sour and Wanjiru says soap is slippery. Why might that be?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Tell learners we will test these ideas with data.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Write-Share: writing a prediction before instruction makes learners' prior ideas visible and gives them something to compare with the evidence later. Recording ideas without judging encourages risk-taking and creates a baseline to revisit when the pH data arrive.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check whether learners (1) give a reason (taste, feel, use) rather than only a guess, (2) distinguish edible items from harmful ones, and (3) name properties such as sour, slippery or bitter. Note in your checklist which learners suggest a number-based or scale-based way to compare. Misconceptions to note: 'all chemicals are dangerous', 'soap is the same as lemon because both clean', or 'clear liquids are the same'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners study the pH graph, a bar graph of pH values measured with a pH meter at 25 °C: lemon juice (Kisumu market) 2.0, vinegar (5% ethanoic acid, shop-bought) 2.8, pure water 7.0 (reference line), baking soda solution (1 spoon in 1 cup water, as used for mandazi) 8.3, bar soap solution (1 spoon shavings in 1 cup water) 10.0. Using a data table, they (1) put the products in order from lowest to highest pH, (2) mark which are below and above the water line at 7, (3) calculate differences, such as lemon juice and vinegar differing by 0.8 and soap and baking soda by 1.7, and (4) match each product with the observations given by the teacher: lemon juice and vinegar taste sour and are safe in food; baking soda tastes bitter/salty and is safe in small amounts in food; soap feels slippery, tastes bitter and is harmful if swallowed. They also note the uses: vinegar for pickling, soap for cleaning, baking soda for raising mandazi, lemon juice for flavour and tea.
framework.teacherMoves: Give each pair a printed graph and observation card. Say: 'Look at the water line at 7. What do you notice about where each product sits?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 pairs for their observation, then 2 more for a different pattern. Prompt: 'Which two products are close together? Which is furthest from water?' Ask: 'Lemon juice is 2.0 and vinegar is 2.8. What is the difference, and does it matter?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Do NOT explain H+ or OH- ions or the 10-fold rule; if asked, say: 'Great question, put it on our Driving Question Board.' Read out the sour and slippery observations clearly and stress that nobody should taste lab chemicals. Circulate and check that learners read the axis correctly.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data-pattern noticing (SEP 4): a structured 'I notice / I wonder' routine, with the graph as the only source of evidence. Ordering products and marking the line at 7 helps learners see that the products fall on both sides of pure water, which is the core idea for classification in later lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for learners who (1) correctly order the products as lemon juice (2.0) < vinegar (2.8) < water (7.0) < baking soda (8.3) < soap (10.0), (2) state that two products are below 7 and two are above 7, (3) calculate differences accurately, and (4) link sour with low values and slippery with high values as a pattern, not yet as an explanation. Common errors: reading the graph from the wrong axis, thinking a higher number means more acidic, or ignoring the water reference.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of four, learners build a hypothesis for each product using a claim-evidence-reasoning frame: 'We think lemon juice is ___ because the graph shows ___ and it tastes ___.' They discuss: Why are lemon juice and vinegar so different from soap, although all look clear or white? Why is vinegar good for pickling kachumbari while soap is good for cleaning? Why can soap be harmful if swallowed while lemon juice is safe? They propose hypotheses about what might be inside each product that makes it behave this way. They then sketch an INITIAL MODEL: four boxes (lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda, soap) showing particles they think are responsible for sourness or slipperiness, using their own symbols and a key. Wrong ideas are welcome at this stage.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Work as a team of scientists. Your hypothesis must use at least one number from the graph.' Circulate and ask: 'What in the data makes you say that?' and 'What might be different inside the lemon juice compared with the soap?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 groups to share one hypothesis each; after each, ask a different group: 'Do you agree or disagree, and what evidence would help?' Introduce the words 'acidic' for values below 7 and 'basic' for values above 7 as labels for the pattern only, and say that 7 is neutral like pure water; do not explain ions. Tell groups: 'Draw what you think is inside, even if you are not sure. We will fix it as we learn.' Collect two or three different models and display them.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with an Initial Model (SEP 2: Developing and Using Models): turning the pattern into a hypothesis and a drawing makes learners' thinking visible and creates a baseline model that is revised in every later lesson. Encouraging unfinished or wrong models makes later revisions meaningful.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check whether hypotheses (1) cite numbers from the graph, (2) connect pH to taste and feel, and (3) suggest something inside the substances (particles, ingredients, e.g. citric acid in lemon juice, fats and sodium hydroxide in soap). Look for models that show different particles for different products. Note misconceptions such as 'soap is slippery because of oil only', 'acids are always dangerous', or 'neutral means harmless'. Do not correct; record them for later lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners read the driving question: 'Does the alkalinity of a substance determine its uses in day to day life? Why are patients with hyperacidity issues given antacid medications?' They write 2 questions each on sticky notes, for example 'Why is lemon sour?' (Otieno), 'Why is soap slippery?' (Wanjiru), 'How is pH measured without a meter?', 'What is in an antacid that helps after eating nyama choma?' In groups they sort the notes into categories such as 'How to tell acid from base', 'What is inside them', 'Uses and safety', and 'Health and medicine', and stick them on the DQB under the driving question. Each group reads out its best question.
framework.teacherMoves: Introduce the board: 'This is our Driving Question Board. It tracks what we wonder and what we learn.' Prompt: 'Think of a nurse in Nairobi giving an antacid to a patient with hyperacidity after eating spicy nyama choma. What would you want to know?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 5 learners to read a question aloud and place it. Ask the class: 'Which questions can we answer by testing? Which need us to learn what is inside the particles?' Link to the KICD key inquiry questions by writing on the board: 'How do we classify substances as acids or bases?' and 'Why are acids and bases important in our day-to-day life?' Tell learners we will return to the board at the end of each lesson, move questions to 'answered', and add new ones. Do not answer any question today.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question-Sorting Routine (SEP 1: Asking Questions): sorting learner questions into categories gives purpose to the learning sequence and shows learners that their curiosity drives the lessons. Linking questions to investigable ideas builds a shared 'need to know'.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count questions per learner. Look for questions that (1) ask 'why' or 'how' rather than only 'what', (2) relate to the phenomenon (taste, feel, pH, safety), and (3) connect to the driving question (uses, antacids, hyperacidity). Note learners who only copy others and prompt them with: 'What did you see on the graph that surprised you?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit their initial model and complete a 'Summary Table' in their notebooks with three columns: What we observed (e.g. lemon juice 2.0 and vinegar 2.8 are below 7; baking soda 8.3 and soap 10.0 are above 7; sour versus slippery), What we learned (the products fall on both sides of pure water at 7, and uses differ), and What we can explain so far (a tentative hypothesis). They add one sentence: 'I think hyperacidity patients get antacids because ___.' They finish by writing a prediction for Lesson 2: 'How could we tell if a substance is an acid or a base without a pH meter?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your model page. Label which products you think are on the acidic side and which are on the basic side.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to read their 'I think hyperacidity patients get antacids because...' statements; accept all and say: 'We will test this idea with evidence.' Ask: 'What is one thing you are still unsure about?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Collect models for comparison later. Preview: 'Next lesson we will classify these same four products using colour changes of litmus and red cabbage.' Remind learners about safety: never taste unknown substances at home or in the lab.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Summary Table and Model Baseline (SEP 2): organising observations, learning and tentative explanations into a table builds a record that learners can compare with their later understanding. A model kept as a baseline reveals the progress of their ideas across the unit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect notebooks and check that (1) the observed column includes accurate pH values and the pattern that two products are below 7 and two are above, (2) the learned column states that products fall on both sides of 7, (3) the explained column holds a tentative idea, even if incomplete, and (4) the model has a key. Use a quick tally: how many learners can place all four products on the correct side of 7? Learners who cannot get extra practice with the graph next lesson.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Did learners notice the pattern around 7 without being told? Which hypotheses about what is inside the products were most common, and which misconceptions (e.g. all acids are dangerous, soap is just oil, clear means the same) will need to be addressed in Lessons 2-5? Did the Kenyan contexts (Kisumu market lemons, mandazi, kachumbari, nyama choma) make the phenomenon feel real? Which learners asked the strongest DQB questions, and which stayed silent? Was WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds used consistently? What will you adjust for Lesson 2, where learners classify the same four products with litmus and red cabbage extract?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that lemon juice (pH 2.0) and vinegar (pH 2.8) have pH values below pure water (pH 7.0), while baking soda solution (pH 8.3) and soap solution (pH 10.0) are above 7. Lemon juice and vinegar taste sour and are safe in food, baking soda tastes bitter/salty and is safe in small amounts in food, and soap feels slippery and is harmful if swallowed.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that products that look alike can be on different sides of 7 on the pH scale, and that their uses (vinegar for pickling, soap for cleaning, baking soda for mandazi, lemon juice for flavour and tea) seem to match their pH, taste and feel.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can so far hypothesise that something different inside lemon juice and vinegar from inside baking soda and soap causes the difference in pH, taste and feel, and that antacids may help hyperacidity because they are on the other side of the scale from stomach acid. We still need evidence to test this idea.

LESSONS.title: Sorting the Kitchen: Classifying Household Substances as Acids or Bases with Litmus and Red Cabbage
LESSONS.aresKeywords: acid, base, alkali, indicator, litmus, red cabbage extract, classification, pH, neutral, hypothesis

slo.purpose: Learners classify lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda solution and bar soap solution as acids or bases using the colour changes of litmus and red cabbage extract, and use this evidence to check the hypotheses they made in Lesson 1.
slo.knowledge: Acids turn blue litmus red and leave red litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue and leave blue litmus blue. Red cabbage extract (purple) turns red/pink in acids, stays purple in water, and turns blue-green to green-yellow in bases. Indicators are substances that show by colour change whether a substance is acidic or basic. Classification must be based on evidence from a pattern of colour changes, not on appearance alone.
slo.skills: Planning and carrying out a fair test (NGSS SEP: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations); recording observations in a results table; analysing and interpreting data to identify patterns (NGSS SEP: Analyzing and Interpreting Data); constructing evidence-based claims (NGSS SEP: Engaging in Argument from Evidence); handling chemicals safely.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about how everyday kitchen substances behave; honesty in recording what is actually observed; respect for safety rules; willingness to revise a hypothesis when evidence disagrees; cooperation in groups.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we classify substances as acids or bases? (KICD Key Inquiry Question 1) Linked to: Why are acids and bases important in our day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1 learners saw the pH graph for lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda and soap and suggested hypotheses about which are acidic or basic. In this lesson they gather their first hands-on evidence: indicator colour changes that sort the four products into two groups. This gives them a classification they can later explain with H+ and OH- ions (Lessons 4-5) and test with other indicators (Lesson 3), and moves them towards answering whether the nature of a substance decides its use.
slo.safetyNotes: Wear goggles and wear aprons. NEVER taste any substance in the laboratory, including the kitchen products, because lab containers and equipment are not food-safe. Use only small volumes (about 2 cm depth in test tubes or small cups). Soap solution may irritate eyes; rinse splashes with plenty of water and tell the teacher. Wash hands after the practical. Dispose of used solutions down the sink with plenty of water. Prepare the red cabbage extract beforehand with warm water, and the teacher handles all hot water.

LESSONS.overview: Mrs Achieng's Kisumu class return to the four products from Lesson 1 (lemon juice from Kisumu market, vinegar, baking soda used by Mama Wanjiru for mandazi, and bar soap), which look alike but behave differently. Learners first predict how litmus paper and purple red cabbage extract will change in each product, using their Lesson 1 hypotheses. They then test each product (plus pure water as a reference) with red litmus, blue litmus and red cabbage extract, and record their results. In the Explain phase they look for patterns in the class data, sort the products into acids and bases, and compare the sorting with their Lesson 1 hypotheses. They add new questions to the Driving Question Board and add a first classification layer to their model (labelling each product as acid or base, with particle drawings of H+ and OH- coming in later lessons).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the four products again (lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda solution, soap solution) and the pH graph from Lesson 1. Otieno's question 'Why is lemon sour?' and Wanjiru's question 'Why is soap slippery?' are read out. Individually, learners write in their notebooks a prediction for each product: will red litmus turn blue, will blue litmus turn red, and what colour will purple red cabbage extract become (red/pink, stay purple, or blue/green)? They write one sentence explaining the reason for their prediction, using ideas from Lesson 1. Then they compare with a partner.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the four products and the pH graph. Say: 'Last lesson you made hypotheses about which of these are acidic and which are basic. Today we will collect evidence to check them. A hypothesis is only useful if we can test it.' Show red litmus, blue litmus and a cup of purple red cabbage extract and say: 'Before we test, write down what you think will happen to each of these in each product, and why.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds of silent thinking before writing begins. Circulate and note common ideas, for example that appearance (clear vs white) decides acidity. Cold-call 3 learners with: 'What do you predict for the soap and why?' Ask 2 more: 'Who predicted something different?' Record the predictions on the board in a prediction table without saying which is correct.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with Reasoning (Predict-Observe-Explain): Writing a prediction and a reason before the experiment makes learners' existing ideas visible. When their results later agree or disagree with the prediction, they have a clear reason to revise their thinking, which builds conceptual change.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check notebooks for: (1) a prediction written for each of the four products; (2) a reason that refers to Lesson 1 evidence (pH below or above 7, sour taste or slippery feel) and not only appearance. Indicator of readiness: at least 80% of learners link low pH or sour taste to 'acid' and higher pH or slippery feel to 'base'. Note learners who predict from appearance alone for extra questioning during the practical.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of four, learners carry out the practical. Roles: Materials manager, Tester, Recorder and Safety/Reporter. They label 5 small cups: lemon juice, vinegar, water, baking soda solution (1 spoon in 1 cup water) and soap solution (1 spoon shavings in 1 cup water). Step 1: Dip a strip of red litmus into each, record the colour. Step 2: Dip a strip of blue litmus into each, record the colour (using a fresh strip each time). Step 3: Add about 10 drops of purple red cabbage extract to about 2 cm of each liquid and record the colour. They record in a results table with columns for substance, red litmus, blue litmus and red cabbage colour. Expected results: red litmus turns blue in baking soda and soap but stays red in lemon juice, vinegar and (for water) unchanged; blue litmus turns red in lemon juice and vinegar but stays blue in baking soda and soap; red cabbage extract is red/pink in lemon juice, pink-red in vinegar, purple in water, blue-green in baking soda and green-yellow in soap. They also compare with their predictions and mark each one correct or incorrect.
framework.teacherMoves: Before starting, demonstrate the safety rules: 'Goggles on. We never taste anything in the lab, even if it is food at home.' Model how to use a fresh strip each time and how to avoid cross-contamination. Say: 'Water is our reference. Why do you think we test water too?' and give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Circulate with questions: 'What colour did the red litmus become in the soap? What does that tell you?' and 'Is this what you predicted?' Challenge: 'Why must we use the same amount of each liquid and the same number of drops?' (fair test). Cold-call 3 groups to report one surprising observation. Check any group whose cabbage colours do not match the expected pattern and ask them to repeat with fresh liquid. Remind groups to record exactly what they see, not what they expect.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Data Collection with a Fair Test: A shared results table and a water control make the evidence systematic and comparable. Learners see the same pattern repeating across three indicators, which supports reliability and starts pattern recognition.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether: (1) each group uses a fresh strip for each liquid; (2) results tables are complete and colours are described accurately (for example 'blue-green', not just 'blue'); (3) water is used as a reference; (4) learners wear goggles and do not taste anything. Indicator of success: at least 4 of 5 rows in a group table match the class pattern. Use a quick checklist and prompt groups with errors to repeat.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups put their results on a large class table on the board (one column per indicator, one row per product). In pairs, learners look for patterns: which products turn red litmus blue and which turn blue litmus red, and how the red cabbage colours group together. They then write a claim: 'Lemon juice and vinegar are ___ because ___; baking soda and soap are ___ because ___.' They use evidence from at least two indicators. They compare the classification with their Lesson 1 hypotheses and the pH graph (lemon 2.0, vinegar 2.8, water 7.0, baking soda 8.3, soap 10.0): did the indicators agree with the pH side of 7? They explain why water is neither (neutral) and discuss why the colour of the cabbage extract is a range rather than just two colours. They then relate the finding to Otieno's and Wanjiru's questions, noting that they know what group each belongs to but not yet why, which is saved for later lessons. They also discuss, with home examples, what the sorting suggests about uses (for example vinegar for pickling kachumbari and onions, soap for cleaning, baking soda for mandazi).
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: 'What pattern do you see across the three indicators? Talk to your partner for two minutes.' Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 4 learners to describe the pattern using evidence. Prompt: 'Which hypothesis from last lesson was supported? Which needs revising?' Use the sentence frame: 'I know lemon juice is an acid because the blue litmus turned ___ and the cabbage extract turned ___.' Challenge misconceptions, for example 'soap is a base because it is not food' or 'white means base': 'Does colour or appearance appear in our evidence? What does our evidence say?' Ask: 'Water stayed purple. Where would you place it?' Introduce the working definitions: 'An indicator is a substance that changes colour to show whether something is acidic or basic. Acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue.' Note that alkali and ion explanations will come later. Do not give the ion explanation yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with Pattern Analysis: Learners state a claim, cite colour-change data from more than one indicator, and give reasoning linking the pattern to the acid/base category. Using multiple indicators strengthens the argument and shows why classification rests on evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect written CER statements. Success criteria: (1) a correct claim for all four products; (2) evidence cited from at least two indicators with correct colours; (3) a reason connecting the colour pattern to acid or base; (4) water identified as neutral. Look for learners who still rely on taste or looks, and plan re-teaching with the data table. Use a thumbs-up/sideways/down check on 'I can classify a substance using litmus'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the Driving Question Board from Lesson 1: 'Does the alkalinity of a substance determine its uses in day to day life? Why are patients with hyperacidity issues given antacid medications?' In groups they write new questions on sticky notes arising from today's evidence, for example 'Why does litmus change colour?', 'Why does red cabbage show many colours?', 'Why does a kitchen product like baking soda behave like soap?', 'How strong is each acid?' and 'Is an antacid an acid or a base?' They place their notes on the DQB under categories (How do we know?, Why does it happen?, What is it used for?) and mark which earlier questions have been partly answered (for example 'Which products are acidic and which basic?').
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at the board. Which of our questions did we make progress on today? Which new questions do you have?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then ask groups to write at least 2 new questions each. Cold-call 3 groups to read a question and say where it goes on the DQB. Highlight a question the class cannot yet answer, such as 'Why does soap feel slippery?', and say: 'That is a great question. We will return to it when we study what is inside these substances.' Tick off or annotate answered questions with a short note, for example 'Lesson 2: classified using litmus and cabbage'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (DQB): Placing new questions publicly connects each lesson's evidence to the unit's big question. It shows learners that their curiosity guides what is investigated next and keeps the phenomenon at the centre.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that each group has produced at least 2 questions that arise from the evidence (not general topic questions). Indicator of progress: questions about causes ('why does the colour change?') or uses ('why use baking soda in mandazi?'), not only recall. Note learners who ask about antacids as an early link to the second part of the driving question.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open the initial model page from Lesson 1 and begin the first version of the class model. Using four boxes (lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda solution, soap solution) plus water, they label each box 'acid' or 'base' (and water 'neutral'), add the colour results for litmus and red cabbage, and write the pH value from the graph (2.0, 2.8, 8.3, 10.0, and 7.0). Where particles are not yet known, they leave a labelled 'we do not know yet' space for what is inside that makes the substance act this way, and draw a question mark. They add a short caption linking one product to its use, such as 'vinegar (acid) is used by mama mboga to pickle kachumbari' or 'baking soda (base) is used for mandazi'. They revise any hypothesis that was not supported.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model should show what we have evidence for. What do we know, and what do we still not know?' Provide WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before drawing. Circulate and ask: 'Which evidence supports the label on this box?' and 'What could be different inside lemon juice and soap?' Cold-call 3 learners to share a label and the evidence behind it. Emphasise that the particle drawings with H+ and OH- will be added in later lessons. Collect model pages to review.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model Building and Revision: Adding evidence-based labels and honest gaps to a visible model helps learners link observations to a developing explanation, and shows that models grow as new evidence is gathered.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check models for: (1) correct labels for all five substances; (2) colour results and pH values placed correctly; (3) a clearly marked unknown area instead of invented explanations; (4) a use linked to the classification. Exit ticket: 'Name one piece of evidence that shows lemon juice is an acid and one that shows soap is a base.' Success is two correct pieces of evidence.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners relied on appearance or taste instead of the indicator evidence, and how did their thinking change after the practical? Did every group use a fair test with a water reference and fresh strips? Were the red cabbage colours distinct enough for learners to see the difference between lemon juice, vinegar and water? Which questions on the DQB show that learners are ready to ask why indicators change colour, and how can I use them in Lessons 3 to 5? Did the classification activity stay linked to the phenomenon and to the idea of use (pickling, mandazi, cleaning)?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Record what you saw: the colour of red litmus, blue litmus and red cabbage extract in lemon juice, vinegar, water, baking soda solution and soap solution.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Write how you can sort a substance as an acid or a base using the pattern of colour changes: acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue; water does not change either.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Explain how the indicator results classify the four kitchen products, how they compare with your Lesson 1 hypotheses and pH values (2.0, 2.8, 7.0, 8.3, 10.0), and what you still want to find out about why they behave this way and how this might affect their uses.

LESSONS.title: Natural and Laboratory Indicators: Building a Classification Table
LESSONS.aresKeywords: indicator, natural indicator, laboratory indicator, universal indicator, red cabbage extract, litmus, phenolphthalein, pH, acid, base, neutral, classification table, hypothesis

slo.purpose: Learners compare natural and laboratory indicators using the four household products and water, and build a classification table (acid, neutral, base) that lets them check and revise their Lesson 1 hypotheses against the pH values.
slo.knowledge: Acids are sour; bases are slippery and bitter. Litmus is red in acids and blue in bases. Phenolphthalein is colourless in acids and pink in bases. Methyl orange is red in acids and yellow in bases. Red cabbage extract is a natural indicator (purple in water, red/pink in acids, blue-green to green-yellow in bases). Universal indicator, a laboratory indicator, gives a range of colours that matches the pH scale (0 to 14; 7 neutral; below 7 acidic; above 7 basic). Pure water is neutral (pH 7.0).
slo.skills: Observing and recording colour changes accurately; comparing the evidence from different indicators; constructing a classification table; analysing data (matching colours to pH values); revising hypotheses using evidence; communicating findings in scientific language (NGSS SEP: Analyzing and Interpreting Data; Constructing Explanations).
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about everyday Kenyan products; respect for evidence when it contradicts an earlier idea; careful and responsible handling of chemicals; cooperation and respect for peers' ideas in group work.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we classify substances as acids or bases? 2. Why are acids and bases important in our day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 2 gave learners a first sort of lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda and soap using litmus and red cabbage. Lesson 3 adds universal indicator (and optional phenolphthalein), puts neutral water into the sort, and links colour to pH values so learners can test the hypotheses from Lesson 1. This gives the classification evidence that Lesson 4 will explain with H+ ions.
slo.safetyNotes: Wear goggles and keep food items out of the lab; never taste any chemical or test solution, including the household products used as test solutions. Use only the household products at the dilutions given (1 spoon in 1 cup water for baking soda and soap). Phenolphthalein, if used, is for the teacher demonstration only. Wipe spills immediately (soap is slippery), wash hands after the practical, and dispose of the test solutions down the sink with plenty of water.

LESSONS.overview: Mrs Achieng returns to the Kisumu market products and the pH graph. Otieno asked 'why is lemon sour?' and Wanjiru asked 'why is soap slippery?', and the class has so far sorted the products with litmus and red cabbage. Today learners predict which colours universal indicator will give, then test lemon juice, vinegar, water, baking soda solution and soap solution with red cabbage extract and universal indicator, and compare the two indicators. Learners explain why different indicators give different colours but the same sorting, build a three-column classification table (acid, neutral, base) that includes water, match colours to the pH values (2.0, 2.8, 7.0, 8.3, 10.0), revise their hypotheses and the Driving Question Board (DQB), and update their particle model with a first claim about which products are likely to have more H+ and which more OH-.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the Lesson 2 litmus and red cabbage sorting (acidic vs basic). Mrs Achieng shows the pH graph and asks: 'Lemon juice is pH 2.0 and vinegar is 2.8. Both are acids, but will they look the same with universal indicator? Where will pure water fit?' In pairs, learners draw a prediction strip of 5 colour boxes (lemon juice, vinegar, water, baking soda, soap) and colour it using a rainbow guess, with a sentence: 'I think ___ will be ___ because ___.' Learners also predict whether water belongs in the acid column, the base column, or neither.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the four products and a glass of water from the Kisumu school tap. Say: 'Yesterday we sorted by litmus. Today water joins the sorting. Where does it go, and how could we tell?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before anyone speaks. Cold-call 4 pairs (not volunteers) to share the colour they predict for lemon juice and why. Record all predictions on the board without judging. Ask: 'Which of the 5 colours do you feel most sure about? Which least sure?' Note learners who say water is acidic or basic, and learners who link low pH to red.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (prediction strip): committing to a prediction makes learners' existing ideas visible, so later evidence either confirms or challenges them. This creates a reason to look carefully at the results and fits the idea of testing hypotheses from Lesson 1.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) at least 8 of 10 pairs commit to a written prediction for all 5 substances; (2) learners use evidence from Lesson 2 (e.g. 'lemon turned blue litmus red so it should be at the red end'); (3) learners place water in a separate or neutral position. Note misconceptions such as 'water has no pH' or 'all acids are the same colour'.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners use 5 labelled test tubes (lemon juice, vinegar, water, baking soda solution, soap solution; as in Lesson 1, the baking soda and soap are 1 spoon in 1 cup water). Step 1: add 2 cm3 of red cabbage extract (purple) to each tube and record the colours. Step 2: in a second set of tubes add 3 drops of universal indicator and compare with the pH colour chart. Expected results: Red cabbage extract: lemon juice red/pink, vinegar pink-red, water purple, baking soda blue-green, soap green-yellow. Universal indicator: lemon juice red-orange (pH 2), vinegar orange (pH 3), water green (7), baking soda blue (8), soap blue-purple (10). The teacher demonstrates phenolphthalein (optional): colourless in lemon juice and vinegar, colourless in water, pink in baking soda and soap solutions. Groups record in a table: substance | red cabbage colour | universal indicator colour | pH from chart.
framework.teacherMoves: Model one tube first: 'Watch carefully as I add three drops to the lemon juice. Describe only what you SEE, not what you think.' Circulate with a checklist; ask each group: 'Which two tubes look most alike with red cabbage? With universal indicator? What does that tell you?' Remind: 'Goggles on. We do not taste, even the lemon juice and vinegar.' Wait 10-15 seconds after asking: 'What do you notice about the order of colours from lemon juice to soap?' Cold-call 3 groups to read out their colour for water. Point to the pH graph to show that the chart readings (pH 2, 3, 7, 8, 10) are close to the pH meter values (2.0, 2.8, 7.0, 8.3, 10.0), and explain that the chart is read by colour, so it gives whole numbers while the meter gives more exact values.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured data collection with a shared observation table: separating observation (colour seen) from interpretation (acid or base) trains learners to use evidence rather than assumptions, and comparing two indicators on the same samples shows what each indicator adds.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) groups record colours for all 5 substances with both indicators; (2) learners use descriptive colour terms (red-orange, blue-green) rather than 'it changed'; (3) learners notice that water is purple with red cabbage and green with universal indicator, unlike the other four; (4) learners safely handle tubes and keep goggles on. Ask one learner per group to point to the tube that gave the lowest pH reading.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners build a class classification table with three columns: Acid (pH below 7), Neutral (pH 7), Base (pH above 7). Under each substance they list: indicator colours (litmus from Lesson 2, red cabbage, universal indicator), pH value (from the graph), taste/feel observation (sour, bitter, slippery) and everyday use (vinegar for pickling kachumbari, soap for cleaning, baking soda for mandazi, lemon for tea). Learners then compare indicators: red cabbage extract is a natural indicator made from a plant; universal indicator is a laboratory indicator; litmus is a laboratory indicator (from lichen). Groups answer: (a) Why is the sorting the same with all indicators but the colours differ? (b) Which indicator tells us how acidic or basic, not just which side? (c) Which of our Lesson 1 hypotheses were supported or need revising? Learners write a claim-evidence-reasoning statement, e.g. 'Lemon juice is more acidic than vinegar because universal indicator is red-orange (pH 2) while vinegar is orange (pH 3), and the graph shows 2.0 and 2.8.'
framework.teacherMoves: Draw the empty table and ask groups to propose entries; say: 'Where does water go and what is your evidence?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 5 learners, one for each substance, to place it and give the evidence. Probe: 'Litmus only told us acid or base. What extra information did universal indicator give us?' Ask: 'Otieno asked why lemon is sour. Can the table answer that yet?' (Expected: not yet; the table shows that it is acidic, not why it is sour. Park for the DQB.) Ask learners to compare their Lesson 1 hypotheses with the table: 'Which hypothesis do you keep, and which do you change?' Clarify the convention: acid produces H+ (aq) in water; do NOT explain ions in depth, as that is for Lesson 4. Note that red cabbage is an everyday natural indicator that can be extracted from the kitchen, whereas litmus and universal indicator come from the lab.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with a classification table: organising multiple lines of evidence in one table lets learners see patterns (low pH = red/orange = acid; high pH = blue/purple = base; water in the middle) and justify classifications with data. Comparing hypotheses with evidence builds the habit of revising ideas.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) the table has water correctly in the neutral column with pH 7.0 and a green universal indicator colour; (2) learners cite at least 2 pieces of evidence per classification; (3) learners state that lemon juice (pH 2.0) is more acidic than vinegar (pH 2.8), and soap (10.0) more basic than baking soda (8.3); (4) learners revise at least one hypothesis in writing. Use an exit slip: 'Name one advantage of universal indicator over litmus.' Expected: it shows the strength (pH value), not only acid or base.

framework.learnerExperience: At the Driving Question Board, learners add sticky notes in two colours: green = 'What we now know' and yellow = 'New questions'. Possible green notes: 'Water is neutral, pH 7.0', 'Lemon juice has a lower pH than vinegar', 'Indicators change colour depending on whether a substance is acid or base.' Possible yellow questions: 'Why is lemon juice sour but soap slippery?' (Otieno and Wanjiru), 'Why do indicators change colour?', 'What does pH 2 mean compared with pH 3?', 'If soap is a base, why do antacids also count as bases?', 'Why are patients with hyperacidity given antacids?' Learners link each note to the driving question by drawing an arrow towards 'Does the alkalinity of a substance determine its uses in day to day life?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take two minutes to write one thing we have learned and one question we still have.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before collecting. Cold-call 4 learners to read and place a note, and ask the class: 'Does this question connect to uses, to safety, or to antacids?' Cluster the questions into themes (why colour changes, what pH means, safety/uses, antacids). Highlight questions that will be answered in Lesson 4 (what makes acids sour; H+ ions) and later lessons, saying: 'We will come back to this question in a coming lesson.' Keep the board visible for revisiting.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with Know/Wonder notes: showing both progress and open questions keeps the phenomenon at the centre of the unit and gives learners ownership of the next steps.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) every learner contributes at least one note; (2) at least some questions move from 'what' towards 'why' (e.g. why indicators change colour, why soap is slippery); (3) learners link notes to the driving question on the board; (4) learners connect antacid use to the classification of bases.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open their model page: a particle drawing of H+ and OH- ions in each product (lemon juice, vinegar, water, baking soda solution, soap solution). Using the classification table and pH values, they make a first draft: lemon juice (pH 2.0) with many H+ ions, vinegar (pH 2.8) with fewer H+ than lemon, water with equal very few H+ and OH-, baking soda (pH 8.3) with more OH- than H+, soap (pH 10.0) with the most OH-. They add a key and a caption in their own words, e.g. 'Lower pH likely means more H+; higher pH likely means more OH-' and label which indicator colour matches each beaker. Learners write one 'I wonder' about how the indicator 'knows' the ions are there, to be explored in Lessons 4 and 5.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use your table to decide how many H+ and OH- dots to draw. We have not measured ions yet, so mark your drawing as a first idea.' Circulate with prompts: 'Why did you draw more H+ in lemon juice than vinegar? What evidence are you using?' and 'How did you show that water is neutral?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 3 learners to explain one beaker to the class. Accept qualitative drawings; do not give exact ion counts or teach the Arrhenius definition in detail, as that is for Lessons 4 and 5. Ask learners to add the label 'Draft 1 - Lesson 3' and keep the model for revision.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model building (draft particle model): turning classification data into a visual model helps learners link observable evidence (indicator colours, pH) to particle-level ideas, and starting with a draft encourages revision as new evidence arrives.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) models show more H+ for the acids than the bases and more OH- for the bases than the acids; (2) lemon juice is shown as more acidic than vinegar; (3) water is shown as neutral, with equal small amounts of H+ and OH-; (4) learners label their model as a draft and give a reason from the evidence. Use a 3-2-1 check: 3 products classified, 2 pieces of evidence, 1 remaining question.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Reflect: (1) Did learners place water correctly using evidence rather than guessing? (2) Could learners explain why different indicators give different colours but the same classification? (3) Did learners distinguish observation from interpretation when recording colours? (4) Which hypotheses from Lesson 1 were revised, and did any learners resist changing them? (5) Did every learner contribute to the DQB, including quieter learners? (6) Are learners over-interpreting their ion drawings as exact numbers? Plan to revisit any misconceptions at the start of Lesson 4, when the Arrhenius definition of acids is introduced using the H+ concentrations of lemon juice and vinegar.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We tested lemon juice, vinegar, water, baking soda solution and soap solution with red cabbage extract and universal indicator. Red cabbage: lemon juice red/pink, vinegar pink-red, water purple, baking soda blue-green, soap green-yellow. Universal indicator: lemon juice red-orange (pH 2), vinegar orange (pH 3), water green (7), baking soda blue (8), soap blue-purple (10).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Indicators show whether a substance is acidic, neutral or basic. Natural indicators such as red cabbage extract and laboratory indicators such as litmus and universal indicator all give the same sorting, even though the colours differ. Universal indicator also shows how acidic or basic a substance is on the pH scale. Water is neutral (pH 7.0).
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Lemon juice (pH 2.0) and vinegar (pH 2.8) are acids; baking soda (pH 8.3) and soap (pH 10.0) are bases; water (pH 7.0) is neutral. Lemon juice is more acidic than vinegar, and soap is more basic than baking soda. Our hypotheses from Lesson 1 are supported by the indicator evidence and the pH values, and our model shows more H+ in the acids and more OH- in the bases. We still need to explain why acids are sour and soap is slippery.
