LESSONS.title: Strength of Acids and Bases and the pH Scale
LESSONS.aresKeywords: strong acid, weak acid, strong base, weak base, degree of ionisation, pH scale, universal indicator, concentration, H+ (aq), OH- (aq), hyperacidity, antacid

slo.purpose: To help learners use universal indicator and the pH scale to compare strong and weak acids and bases, and to explain that strength depends on how much a substance ionises in water, which is different from how much is dissolved (concentration).
slo.knowledge: Learners will be able to: (1) use universal indicator colours and pH values to rank acids and bases by strength; (2) explain that a strong acid or base ionises almost completely in water while a weak one ionises only partly; (3) distinguish strength from concentration; (4) interpret that each pH unit is a 10-fold change in H+ concentration, so lemon juice (pH 2.0) has about 6 times more H+ (aq) than vinegar (pH 2.8).
slo.skills: Planning and carrying out investigations (NGSS SEP 3); analysing and interpreting data (SEP 4); using mathematics and computational thinking (10-fold change per pH unit) (SEP 5); developing and using models (SEP 2), drawing particle diagrams of H+ and OH- ions; practical skills in using universal indicator safely, observing, recording and comparing.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate that precise, evidence-based comparison (pH values rather than just 'sour' or 'slippery') is needed to decide how a substance is used safely. They show curiosity, careful teamwork and respect for laboratory safety rules.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we classify substances as acids or bases? 2. Why are acids and bases important in our day-to-day life? (Focus today: how do we tell how strong an acid or base is, and why does strength matter for use and safety?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 3-5 gave us indicators and the idea that acids release H+ (aq) and alkalis release OH- (aq). Lesson 7 showed antacids neutralising stomach hydrochloric acid. Lesson 8 now asks: do all acids behave the same? Learners find that acids and bases differ in strength, which refines the particle model (more or fewer ions) and prepares for Lesson 9 (uses and safety) and Lesson 10 (answering the driving question).
slo.safetyNotes: Wear goggles and lab coats or aprons. Never taste any laboratory chemical. Use only 0.1 M solutions of hydrochloric acid, ethanoic acid, sodium hydroxide and ammonia, pre-prepared by the teacher. Sodium hydroxide is corrosive: handle with care and rinse spills with plenty of water. Ammonia has a pungent smell: keep tubes at arm's length, work in a ventilated room and do not sniff directly. Use dropper amounts only. Household samples (lemon juice, vinegar) may be used but must not be tasted in the lab. Wash hands after the practical.

LESSONS.overview: Back in Mwalimu Achieng's classroom in Kisumu, the pH graph shows lemon juice at pH 2.0 and vinegar at pH 2.8, both acidic and both sour. Otieno asks: 'If both are acids, why is lemon juice lower on the graph?' Learners predict how acids and bases of the same concentration compare, then test 0.1 M hydrochloric acid, 0.1 M ethanoic acid (acetic acid), 0.1 M sodium hydroxide and 0.1 M ammonia solution with universal indicator. The data show HCl pH 1 versus ethanoic acid pH 3, and NaOH pH 13 versus ammonia pH 11. Learners explain the difference through ionisation, separate strength from concentration, calculate the 10-fold change per pH unit for lemon juice versus vinegar, link strength to antacid choice for hyperacidity (stomach hydrochloric acid, pH about 1.5 to 2), add questions to the Driving Question Board, and revise their particle model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look again at the pH graph from the phenomenon (lemon juice 2.0, vinegar 2.8, water 7.0, baking soda 8.3, soap 10.0). Individually they write a prediction in their notebooks: 'Two acids of the same concentration, 0.1 M hydrochloric acid and 0.1 M ethanoic acid, are tested with universal indicator. Will they have the same pH? Why or why not?' They do the same for 0.1 M sodium hydroxide and 0.1 M ammonia solution. They sketch a quick prediction on a pH strip from 0 to 14 showing where they think each will fall. Pairs compare predictions and note disagreements.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the pH graph and say: 'Lemon juice and vinegar are both acids and both sour, yet lemon juice is at pH 2.0 and vinegar at 2.8. Otieno asked why they are not the same. Today we find out what makes one acid stronger than another.' Give 3 minutes of silent writing. Say: 'Write your prediction and one reason. I am not marking right or wrong.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after asking: 'Who thinks the two acids will have the same pH?' Take a show of hands, then cold-call 3 learners with different predictions: 'Wanjiru, what made you choose that?' Record the class split on the board (same / different) without judging. Ask: 'What could we measure to settle this?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with reasoning (Predict-Observe-Explain): by committing to a prediction and a reason, learners expose their current ideas, such as 'same concentration means same acidity', so that the later evidence creates a productive conflict they must resolve.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check notebooks for: (a) a clear prediction (same or different) for each pair; (b) a stated reason; (c) a pH strip sketch with the acids on the left of 7 and the bases on the right. Tally how many learners assume that equal concentration means equal pH. Look for the misconception 'strong means concentrated'. Note it for the Explain Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners wearing goggles carry out a practical. They add 3 drops of universal indicator to 2 cm3 of each pre-prepared 0.1 M solution in labelled test tubes: hydrochloric acid, ethanoic acid, sodium hydroxide and ammonia solution. They also test lemon juice and vinegar from the phenomenon. They match the colour to the universal indicator pH chart and record the pH in a table: HCl pH 1 (red), ethanoic acid pH 3 (orange), NaOH pH 13 (purple), ammonia pH 11 (blue-purple), lemon juice pH 2 (red-orange), vinegar pH 3 on the indicator chart (orange; pH meter value 2.8), and water pH 7 (green) as a reference. Each group plots the results on a class pH scale chart (0 to 14). They also observe that the HCl and ethanoic acid have the SAME concentration (0.1 M) but DIFFERENT pH, and likewise for NaOH and ammonia.
framework.teacherMoves: Before the practical, review the rules: 'Goggles on before anyone touches a tube. We never taste lab chemicals.' Demonstrate 3 drops, with the tube held at arm's length when testing ammonia. Circulate and ask each group: 'What colour do you see, and what pH does the chart give?' and 'Both tubes contain 0.1 M. What do you notice about the colours?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before accepting an answer. Ask a group to read the data aloud, and cold-call 4 groups to report one result each to fill the class table. Provide pre-measured quantities and check that the sodium hydroxide is handled carefully. Remind: 'Compare to the pH chart in good light, against a white paper.' Reference the phenomenon: 'Does the pH of the lab acid match the pH of the lemon juice and vinegar we had in Lesson 1?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data table and number line (pH scale) construction: arranging all substances on one 0-14 scale makes patterns visible (strong acids near 0-1, weak acids near 3-6, weak bases near 8-11, strong bases near 13-14) and lets learners compare strength using evidence rather than taste.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners: (a) wear goggles and handle droppers correctly; (b) read the colour chart accurately (HCl pH 1, ethanoic acid pH 3, NaOH pH 13, ammonia pH 11); (c) record results in the correct units/format; (d) notice that equal concentration gave unequal pH. Use a checklist during circulation. Ask one probing question per group and note correct and incorrect answers.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners analyse their data to answer: 'Why do 0.1 M HCl and 0.1 M ethanoic acid have different pH values?' The teacher introduces the idea of degree of ionisation with a particle drawing. In HCl nearly every molecule splits into H+ (aq) and Cl- (aq), so there are many H+ ions and pH is 1. In ethanoic acid (acetic acid) only a few molecules ionise and most stay as whole molecules, so there are fewer H+ ions and pH is 3. The same reasoning is applied to the bases: NaOH ionises almost completely into Na+ and OH- (aq) (pH 13), while ammonia produces fewer OH- (aq) (pH 11). Learners complete a sentence frame: 'A strong acid ______ while a weak acid ______.' Then they separate strength from concentration: a dilute strong acid and a concentrated weak acid are discussed with a Kenyan example (a very watery HCl versus strong vinegar). Finally they use the pH graph: each pH unit is a 10-fold change in H+ concentration, so lemon juice (pH 2.0, 1 x 10^-2 mol/L) has about 6 times more H+ than vinegar (pH 2.8, about 1.6 x 10^-3 mol/L), since the difference of 0.8 pH units gives 10^0.8 ≈ 6.3. They also compare soap (10.0) and baking soda (8.3), a difference of 1.7, and explain that soap is the stronger base in this comparison. Learners link this to Lesson 7: a pharmacist in Nairobi chooses an antacid such as magnesium hydroxide, a weak base, which neutralises excess stomach hydrochloric acid (pH about 1.5 to 2) and raises the pH to about 3.5 to 5 without making the stomach strongly basic like a strong base such as NaOH would.
framework.teacherMoves: Pose: 'Both tubes had 0.1 M. If concentration is the same, what else could cause a different pH?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then Think-Pair-Share for 2 minutes. Cold-call 3 pairs. Draw on the board two beakers: one with nearly all molecules split into H+ and Cl-, one with few molecules split. Say: 'Strength is about how much of the acid ionises, not how much is dissolved.' Use the analogy of 10 learners in a class: in a strong acid almost all 10 leave their seats (ionise), in a weak acid only 1 or 2 leave. Clarify language: 'Strong does not mean concentrated, and weak does not mean dilute.' Write on the board: pH 2.0 to 2.8 is a difference of 0.8, so 10^0.8 ≈ 6.3, about 6 times. Ask: 'If one pH unit is 10 times, what would a difference of 2 units be?' (100 times) Cold-call 3 learners to explain. Address the misconception that Otieno raised: 'Lemon juice has more H+ than vinegar, so it is more acidic, though both are weak acids.' Ask: 'Why do pharmacists in Nairobi prefer magnesium hydroxide, a weak base, to NaOH for hyperacidity?' Stress safety: NaOH is corrosive and must never be swallowed. Do not re-teach neutralisation itself (Lesson 7); use it as the application.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with particle modelling: learners claim that HCl is stronger than ethanoic acid, cite pH data as evidence, and use the ionisation model (more or fewer ions) as reasoning. Analogies and the 10-fold mathematical rule help them move from observation to a mechanism.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect exit-slip style responses: (a) 'Complete: HCl has a lower pH than ethanoic acid at the same concentration because ______.' (b) 'True or false: a strong acid is always concentrated. Explain.' (c) 'Lemon juice (2.0) vs vinegar (2.8): how many times more H+?' (about 6). Success indicators: uses the words ionise/ionisation, states that the number of H+ (aq) ions is different, separates strength from concentration, and calculates correctly. Reteach in small groups if fewer than 70% give an acceptable answer.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the DQB, which has the main question: 'Does the alkalinity of a substance determine its uses in day to day life? Why are patients with hyperacidity issues given antacid medications?' They review earlier questions (for example Otieno's 'Why is lemon sour?' and Wanjiru's 'Why is soap slippery?'). They mark questions that have been partly answered with evidence from this lesson, such as 'Why is lemon juice lower in pH than vinegar?' They write new questions on sticky notes, for example: 'Is a strong acid always more dangerous?', 'Why does soap, at pH 10, feel safe on the skin but NaOH, at pH 13, burns?', 'Why is the weak base in antacids better than a strong base?', 'How does the farmer in Kericho know how much lime to add?' and place them on the board under the headings 'Answered', 'Partly answered' and 'New'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our DQB. Which questions can we now answer with evidence from today?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to move a question and give the evidence ('What data from today supports moving it?'). Then say: 'Write one new question that today's results made you wonder about, and link it to a product from our kitchen or a place in Kenya.' Invite 4 learners to read their questions aloud and group similar ones (strength and safety, strength and uses). Ask: 'Which of these will we investigate in Lesson 9 on uses and safety?' Mark the answered ones with the lesson number.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question tracking and categorising: showing which questions have been answered, partly answered or newly raised keeps learners accountable for evidence and makes progress toward the driving question visible and student-owned.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the sticky notes: (a) Do new questions use strength, ionisation or pH ideas? (b) Are questions linked to the anchoring phenomenon? (c) Can learners justify moving a question by citing specific data (for example 'HCl pH 1, ethanoic acid pH 3')? Note learners who only restate old questions and prompt them with 'What did you see today that surprised you?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise their particle drawings of H+ and OH- ions for each product from earlier lessons. On a new page they add a 'strength' section. For each of four beakers (0.1 M HCl, 0.1 M ethanoic acid, 0.1 M NaOH, 0.1 M ammonia) they draw the ions and the whole molecules that did not ionise, using more H+ (aq) or OH- (aq) for strong substances and fewer for weak ones. They add a labelled pH scale (0 to 14) with the household products (lemon juice 2.0, vinegar 2.8, water 7.0, baking soda 8.3, soap 10.0) and the lab solutions. They write a caption under lemon juice and vinegar: 'pH 2.0 has about 6 times more H+ than pH 2.8.' They add a note explaining why a weak base such as magnesium hydroxide is used for hyperacidity. Learners compare models in pairs, then add one new feature and one question they still have.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Revise your model so that someone from another class could tell which acid is stronger just by looking at your drawing.' Provide a model-checking list on the board: (1) are H+ (aq) and OH- (aq) clearly labelled? (2) do strong substances show almost complete ionisation and weak ones only a few ions with many whole molecules? (3) does the pH scale include all products? (4) is the 10-fold rule shown? Note that H3O+ is simply another way of writing H+ (aq) in water. Circulate and ask: 'Why did you draw fewer ions here?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to explain their model to the class. Close with: 'What does our model now say about lemon juice and vinegar? And what can it not yet explain?' Link to Lesson 9: 'Next we will use strength and safety to decide how acids and bases are used.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with peer critique: redrawing the particle model and comparing it with a partner's forces learners to turn the abstract idea of ionisation into a visible representation and to test it against the evidence (pH data).
framework.formativeAssessment: Look at the models for: (a) correct ion counts (strong = many ions, weak = few ions plus intact molecules); (b) accurate pH placement of all substances; (c) correct use of H+ (aq), OH- (aq); (d) the 10-fold rule applied to lemon juice and vinegar; (e) an explanation of strength distinct from concentration. Use a 3-level rubric (emerging, developing, secure) and record who needs support before Lesson 9.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners still believe that 'strong' means 'concentrated'? Did the HCl versus ethanoic acid data (pH 1 versus pH 3 at 0.1 M) create enough conflict for them to question that idea? Were the particle drawings clear enough for learners to link pH to the number of ions? How well did learners manage the 10-fold calculation (lemon juice about 6 times more H+ than vinegar)? Was the practical safe and well organised, particularly the handling of sodium hydroxide and ammonia? What adjustments will help learners connect strength to safety and uses in Lesson 9?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: With universal indicator, 0.1 M hydrochloric acid showed pH 1 and 0.1 M ethanoic acid showed pH 3; 0.1 M sodium hydroxide showed pH 13 and 0.1 M ammonia showed pH 11. Lemon juice (pH 2.0) is lower than vinegar (pH 2.8) on the pH graph.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Strength is about the degree of ionisation, not concentration. A strong acid or base ionises almost completely, while a weak one ionises only partly. Each pH unit is a 10-fold change in H+ concentration, so lemon juice has about 6 times more H+ (aq) than vinegar.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: At equal concentration, HCl gives many more H+ (aq) ions than ethanoic acid, so its pH is lower; NaOH gives more OH- (aq) than ammonia, so its pH is higher. This helps explain why a weak base like magnesium hydroxide is a safer antacid for hyperacidity than a strong base, and it advances our answer that alkalinity, together with strength and safety, influences how products are used.

LESSONS.title: Uses of Acids and Bases and Safety: Why Vinegar Pickles, Soap Cleans, Lime Heals Soil and Antacids Soothe
LESSONS.aresKeywords: uses of acids, uses of bases, food preservation, pickling, cleaning, lime, acidic soil, antacid, hyperacidity, neutralisation, safety precautions, pH

slo.purpose: Learners evaluate how the chemical properties of acids and bases (pH, H+ (aq) or OH- (aq) ions, reactions and strength) lead to their uses in food preservation, cleaning, baking, farming and medicine, and decide which safety precautions each use requires. This advances the driving question: Does the alkalinity of a substance determine its uses in day to day life?
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson learners should be able to: (1) link the acidic nature of vinegar (pH 2.8) and lemon juice (pH 2.0) to their uses in pickling and flavour; (2) link the basic nature of soap (pH 10.0) and baking soda (pH 8.3) to cleaning and baking mandazi; (3) explain how lime raises the pH of acidic soil in Kericho from about 4.5 to about 6.0 by neutralisation; (4) explain that antacids (magnesium hydroxide) are bases that neutralise excess stomach hydrochloric acid, raising stomach pH from about 1.5-2 to about 3.5-5; (5) state safety precautions that match the strength and nature of each substance.
slo.skills: Analysing and interpreting data (NGSS SEP 4); Constructing explanations (SEP 6); Engaging in argument from evidence (SEP 7); Evaluating and communicating information (SEP 8); Developing and using models (SEP 2); Critical thinking and decision making.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the importance of acids and bases in everyday Kenyan life; show responsibility and care when handling household and laboratory chemicals; value respect for evidence and for each other's reasoning; show curiosity about how chemistry supports farming, health and food.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we classify substances as acids or bases? 2. Why are acids and bases important in our day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1-8 gave learners the classification of the four products (litmus, red cabbage, universal indicator), the Arrhenius ideas of H+ (aq) and OH- (aq), reactions of acids with metals and carbonates, neutralisation and antacids, and strength versus concentration. Lesson 9 asks the 'so what?' question: do these properties actually decide how each product is used, and what precautions follow? It collects the use-evidence learners need for Lesson 10, where they will write the final evidence-based claim answering the driving question.
slo.safetyNotes: Never taste any laboratory chemical or any household product used in the activity; the sour/slippery observations from Lesson 1 are discussed from the teacher's earlier demonstration only. Wear goggles and keep hands away from the eyes. Use only dilute, household-strength materials (vinegar, lemon juice, baking soda solution, soap solution, small amounts of garden lime in a closed bag). Lime (calcium hydroxide/calcium oxide) irritates skin and eyes: the teacher handles it and learners use only the pH data cards. Keep soap, lime and antacid tablets away from young children. Never mix household cleaners. Wash hands after the lesson and clean spills with plenty of water.

LESSONS.overview: Mrs Achieng returns to the four products on display in the Kisumu classroom: lemon juice (pH 2.0), vinegar (pH 2.8), baking soda solution (pH 8.3) and soap solution (pH 10.0), with water (pH 7.0) as the reference line. Learners already know which are acids and which are bases, and why. Now they ask: do these properties decide how each product is used? In a Predict phase, learners guess which product would be best for four jobs: preserving kachumbari onions, cleaning greasy sufuria, raising mandazi and fixing acidic soil. In the Observe phase they rotate through four evidence stations (Mama mboga's pickling, soap cleaning, Mr Kamau's lime in Kericho, and the nurse/pharmacist in Nairobi giving antacids after spicy nyama choma) and record data in a use-property-safety table. In the Explain phase they build claim-evidence-reasoning statements linking property to use and then evaluate safety precautions, including why soap is harmful if swallowed even though it is useful. They add new questions and answers to the DQB, and revise their particle model of H+ and OH- ions to show what each ion does in the use (for example OH- (aq) from lime reacting with H+ (aq) in soil). Lesson 10 will then bring everything together into the final answer.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the four products and the pH graph from Lesson 1 (lemon juice 2.0, vinegar 2.8, water 7.0, baking soda 8.3, soap 10.0). Otieno asks, 'If lemon juice is so sour, can we use it to wash dishes?' and Wanjiru asks, 'Why is vinegar not used to make mandazi rise?' Learners get a prediction card with four jobs: (a) keeping kachumbari onions from spoiling, (b) removing grease from a sufuria, (c) making mandazi rise and soften, (d) helping maize grow in the acidic tea soil of Kericho (pH about 4.5), plus (e) relieving hyperacidity after nyama choma. Individually, for each job they write which product or type (acid or base) they would choose and why, then pair-share and draw a quick sketch of the ions (H+ or OH-) they think do the work.
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up each product and say, 'These all sit in the same kitchen, but would any one of them do every job? Pick the job, then pick the product. Write your reasoning, not just your answer.' Read the five jobs aloud slowly. Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds of silent thinking before anyone writes. Circulate and note the ideas on a clipboard. Cold-call 4 learners (one per job) with, 'Tell us your prediction and one reason from our earlier lessons.' Do NOT confirm or correct. Say, 'Interesting. We will test that with evidence today.' Record 2-3 predictions in a 'Our predictions' column on the board, including any misconception such as 'all acids are dangerous and useless' or 'bases are always harmful'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with reasoning (Think-Pair-Share): writing a prediction and a reason before instruction makes learners activate Lessons 1-8 (classification, ions, neutralisation, strength) and exposes misconceptions that the evidence stations can later confirm or challenge. Pair-sharing lets learners hear alternative ideas before committing.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners who link a use to acid or base nature (for example 'soap is a base, so it cleans'); (2) learners who mention neutralisation for soil or antacid; (3) learners who use pH numbers from the graph; (4) learners who give only taste or appearance as reasons (needs follow-up); (5) learners who mix up strength with concentration. Tally on a clipboard how many of the 5 jobs each learner matches to acid or base nature; target at least 3 of 5 with a reason. Learners who score below 3 receive a prompt during the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4, learners rotate through four 8-minute evidence stations using data cards, photographs and safe demonstrations, and complete a Use-Property-Safety table. STATION 1 Pickling (acid): vinegar (5% ethanoic acid (acetic acid), pH 2.8) used by mama mboga for kachumbari and onions; a sealed jar of onions in vinegar vs onions in water (prepared two days earlier by the teacher) are compared for smell and appearance; learners record how the low pH and H+ (aq) of vinegar make the environment unsuitable for many spoilage microbes, and note that lemon juice (pH 2.0) is used for flavour and tea. STATION 2 Cleaning and baking (bases): learners test greasy oil on a plate with water, vinegar, and soap solution (pH 10.0) and compare how well each lifts the grease; they also read the recipe card where Mama Wanjiru uses baking soda (pH 8.3) in mandazi and note that vinegar + baking soda produced CO2 in Lesson 6, so baking soda releasing CO2 helps dough rise. STATION 3 Farming: Mr Kamau's tea/maize farm in Kericho; a data card shows soil pH about 4.5 before lime and about 6.0 after liming, with a closed bag of lime shown by the teacher only. Learners use a soil pH strip card to place 4.5 and 6.0 on the pH scale and model the neutralisation of H+ (aq) in the soil by OH- (aq) or carbonate from lime. STATION 4 Medicine: a card shows a patient in Nairobi with hyperacidity after eating spicy nyama choma; stomach acid is hydrochloric acid, pH about 1.5-2; a pharmacist gives a magnesium hydroxide antacid, raising the pH to about 3.5-5. Learners fill the table: use, nature (acid/base), property that explains the use, and safety precaution (for example vinegar: dilute, keep from eyes; soap: do not swallow, keep from children; lime: wear gloves and goggles; antacid: follow the dose, because too much gives side effects).
framework.teacherMoves: Before rotation say, 'Each station asks the same three questions: What is the use? Which property of the substance makes it work? What could go wrong if we are careless?' Assign roles (reader, recorder, reporter, safety officer). Set a timer for 8 minutes per station. Circulate and ask at least two groups per station: 'Where on the pH scale is this? Which ion, H+ (aq) or OH- (aq), is doing the work?' At Station 3 ask, 'What happens to the H+ (aq) in the soil when lime is added? Where have we seen this before?' (neutralisation, Lesson 7). At Station 4 ask, 'How does the antacid change the stomach pH, and why does it not go to pH 7 or higher?' Allow WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Remind groups: 'No tasting anything. Safety officers, check goggles.' If a group is stuck, point to the pH graph instead of giving the answer.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data-rich Gallery Rotation with a structured Use-Property-Safety table (Analysing and Interpreting Data, SEP 4): the same three questions at every station make learners search for a pattern across very different contexts (food, cleaning, farming, medicine), so they see that one idea (the acid or base nature, as shown by pH and ions) explains many uses. Comparing treated and untreated samples (onions, soil pH 4.5 vs 6.0, stomach pH 1.5-2 vs 3.5-5) supports cause-and-effect reasoning.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether each group's table (1) correctly labels each substance as acid or base using the pH data; (2) gives a property-based reason for the use instead of 'because it is useful'; (3) quotes numbers accurately (vinegar 2.8, soap 10.0, baking soda 8.3, soil 4.5 to about 6.0, stomach 1.5-2 to about 3.5-5); (4) gives a safety precaution that matches the substance. Use a 4-item checklist per group. Listen for the safety officer's checks. Common errors to note: saying lime 'makes the soil sweet' without reference to neutralisation; saying all bases are safe to swallow because antacids are bases.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner writes Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) statements for two uses of their choice, for example: Claim: 'Vinegar is suitable for pickling kachumbari.' Evidence: 'It has pH 2.8, lower than water (7.0), and contains H+ (aq) ions from ethanoic acid.' Reasoning: 'The acidic conditions help prevent spoilage, and vinegar is safe in food at 5% strength.' Then in groups they run a 'Safety Courtroom' on soap: Is soap a good product or a dangerous product? They argue for both, using that soap at pH 10.0 has OH- (aq) of 1 x 10^-4 mol/L, removes grease and is useful, but is harmful if swallowed, so the precaution is storage and use for washing only. Next, they compare strong and weak: Why is a weak acid (vinegar, ethanoic acid pH 3 at 0.1 M) safe in food but a strong acid (0.1 M HCl pH 1) is not, and why a weak base like magnesium hydroxide is chosen for antacids instead of a strong base such as sodium hydroxide (pH 13)? Finally, learners return to the driving question and propose: 'Does alkalinity determine use?' They conclude (with evidence) that nature, strength and safety together determine the use.
framework.teacherMoves: Model one CER aloud on the board using Mama Wanjiru's mandazi, then say, 'Now you do one about a job you predicted earlier. Which part of your claim could a classmate challenge?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Ask for revisions of earlier predictions: 'Look at your prediction card. Which prediction would you keep, and which would you change? What evidence changed your mind?' Cold-call 5 learners (at least one per use: preservation, cleaning/baking, farming, medicine, safety) to share a claim and a piece of evidence. Press with: 'How do you know it is the pH and not just the look or the smell?' and 'Is strength the same as concentration? Explain with vinegar and HCl.' In the Safety Courtroom, give each side 3 minutes, then ask the whole class: 'Is a substance that is harmful if swallowed still useful? What precaution makes it safe to use?' Address misconceptions directly: 'Acids are not all dangerous (vinegar, lemon juice) and bases are not all safe (soap, lime, sodium hydroxide). Strength and concentration decide the risk.' Do not re-teach neutralisation or strength; point to the Lesson 7 and 8 posters.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning and Argument from Evidence (SEP 6 and 7): the CER frame forces learners to link a use (claim) to data (pH, ions, reactions) and to a chemical principle (reasoning), while the Safety Courtroom lets them weigh benefit against risk and see that strength matters. Explicit return to earlier predictions supports conceptual change.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect CER statements as exit evidence and score with a 3-point rubric: Claim clear (1), evidence uses correct data (1), reasoning links to H+ (aq)/OH- (aq), neutralisation or strength (1). Target: 80% of learners score at least 2 of 3. Listen in the Safety Courtroom for correct use of 'weak vs strong' and 'concentration'. Watch for the misconception 'bases are safe because antacids are bases' or 'weak acid means dilute'; give a targeted follow-up question and revisit at the start of Lesson 10.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board, which shows 'Does the alkalinity of a substance determine its uses in day to day life? Why are patients with hyperacidity issues given antacid medications?' They use sticky notes in two colours: green for questions they can now answer with evidence (for example 'Why is lime added to the soil in Kericho?' with the answer 'It neutralises acidic H+ (aq) and raises the pH from about 4.5 to about 6.0') and yellow for new or unanswered questions (for example 'Why does a patient not take too many antacids?', 'Could we use lemon juice to clean?', 'Are all cleaners basic?'). They attach evidence cards (pickling table, soil pH, antacid pH change) to the relevant questions. In pairs they decide which questions are still open and which will be needed to answer the driving question in Lesson 10.
framework.teacherMoves: Say, 'Look at our DQB. Which questions can we now answer with evidence? Which ones are still open?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to move a sticky note to the answered section and give the evidence in one sentence. Ask Otieno and Wanjiru (or the learners who first raised the questions) to read their original questions and say whether they have changed their answers. Ask, 'Which new question matters most for the driving question about alkalinity and uses?' and have the class vote with a show of hands. Highlight any question about safety or strength for Lesson 10. Keep the DQB visible on the wall.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as a living record of understanding: sorting questions into answered and open makes learning progress visible, connects each piece of evidence to the anchoring phenomenon, and gives learners ownership of what to investigate next.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that learners (1) move at least one question to 'answered' with a correct evidence statement; (2) write at least one new, testable question connected to the phenomenon (not 'what is an acid?'); (3) attach the right evidence card to the right question. Note the number of learners who contribute. Look for learners who can connect the antacid question to neutralisation and the soil question to pH change, and those who still have unanswered strength-versus-concentration questions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out their particle drawing from Lesson 8 (H+ and OH- ions in each product) and revise it to show uses. In groups they draw four mini-models: (1) vinegar in kachumbari with H+ (aq) ions present (low pH 2.8); (2) soap solution with OH- (aq) ions (pH 10.0) around a grease particle; (3) Kericho soil with H+ (aq) before lime (pH about 4.5), and OH- (aq) from lime combining with H+ (aq) to make H2O after liming (pH about 6.0); (4) the stomach with H+ (aq) from hydrochloric acid (pH about 1.5-2) and OH- (aq) from magnesium hydroxide forming water so fewer H+ (aq) remain (pH about 3.5-5). Each model has a key and a one-line caption explaining the use and a safety note. Learners then use a different colour pen to mark 'what changed in my model since Lesson 8' and write one sentence: 'The alkalinity of a substance helps determine its use because ...'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say, 'Take your Lesson 8 model. Today we add what the ions do in real life. Draw first, then label, then write a caption.' Circulate and check that ion counts reflect pH (fewer H+ at higher pH, more OH- in bases). Ask, 'In the soil, where did the H+ (aq) go after lime? How do we show that in your drawing?' and 'Why does your stomach model still have some H+ (aq) left?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Select 2 groups to display their models; cold-call 3 learners from other groups to say one thing that is strong and one suggestion. Note models that show H+ + OH- giving H2O. Do not give a finished model; ask learners to defend their drawing with data (pH values). Close with, 'Next lesson, you will use this model and all your evidence to answer the driving question.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Developing and Using Models (SEP 2) with cumulative revision: updating the particle model each lesson makes the invisible ions visible and lets learners use the same model to explain very different uses (pickling, cleaning, soil, medicine), which strengthens the idea that one chemical principle explains many everyday observations.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each model for: (1) ions drawn in the right numbers or proportions for each pH; (2) correct neutralisation in soil and stomach (H+ + OH- to H2O); (3) a caption that links the ions to the use; (4) a safety note; (5) visible revision using a different colour. Use a 5-point checklist; target at least 4 of 5 for most groups. Photograph or collect a model from each group for Lesson 10. Learners who draw ions inconsistently with pH get a prompt at the start of Lesson 10.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Could learners connect each use to a specific property (pH, H+ (aq) or OH- (aq), neutralisation) rather than just to the name of the product? (2) Which stations produced the strongest evidence-based talk, and which needed more scaffolding? (3) Did learners confuse strong/weak with concentrated/dilute when judging safety (for example vinegar vs 0.1 M HCl, magnesium hydroxide vs sodium hydroxide)? (4) Did every learner contribute to the Safety Courtroom and CER writing, including quieter learners? (5) Were the Kenyan contexts (Kisumu market lemons, mama mboga's kachumbari, Mama Wanjiru's mandazi, Mr Kamau's farm in Kericho, the Nairobi pharmacist) meaningful and accessible to all learners? (6) Which DQB questions remain open, and what evidence will you need to bring to Lesson 10 so that learners can write a final claim about alkalinity, strength and uses? Record the learners who need extra support with the particle model before the consolidation lesson.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Vinegar (pH 2.8) is used by mama mboga to pickle kachumbari and onions; soap solution (pH 10.0) lifts grease; baking soda (pH 8.3) is used for mandazi; lime raises Kericho soil from pH about 4.5 to about 6.0 for maize; a magnesium hydroxide antacid raises stomach pH from about 1.5-2 to about 3.5-5 after spicy nyama choma.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The uses of acids and bases depend on their nature (H+ (aq) or OH- (aq)), their pH and their strength, and each use needs matching safety precautions: acids help preserve and flavour food, bases clean, bake and neutralise acids in soil and in the stomach, and not every acid or base is safe in the same way.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Alkalinity largely determines uses because bases neutralise acids (acid + base gives salt + water): lime neutralises H+ (aq) in acidic soil, antacids neutralise excess hydrochloric acid in hyperacidity, and soap's OH- (aq) helps remove grease, while strength and safety decide how they can be used.

LESSONS.title: Consolidation: Answering the Driving Question – Alkalinity, Uses and Antacids
LESSONS.aresKeywords: claim, evidence, reasoning, final explanation, alkalinity, pH, H+ (aq), OH- (aq), neutralisation, antacid, hyperacidity, strength, lime, Driving Question Board, final model

slo.purpose: To consolidate the whole unit by constructing an evidence-based final explanation that answers the driving question: does the alkalinity of a substance determine its uses in day to day life, and why are patients with hyperacidity given antacid medications?
slo.knowledge: Learners explain that acids (lemon juice pH 2.0, vinegar pH 2.8) release H+ (aq) ions and bases/alkalis (baking soda pH 8.3, soap pH 10.0) neutralise acids or produce OH- (aq) ions, and that these properties, together with strength and safety, determine uses such as pickling, cleaning, baking, liming soil in Kericho and treating hyperacidity. They explain that antacids neutralise stomach hydrochloric acid (acid + base gives salt + water), raising stomach pH from about 1.5 to 2 up to about 3.5 to 5.
slo.skills: Constructing explanations (NGSS SEP 6), engaging in argument from evidence (SEP 7), developing and using models (SEP 2), interpreting data (SEP 4), communicating scientific information (SEP 8).
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the role of chemistry in health, home and farming; show respect for peers' ideas when critiquing claims; and practise safety awareness when handling household acids and bases.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do we classify substances as acids or bases? 2. Why are acids and bases important in our day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the culminating lesson. Learners return to the Kisumu kitchen phenomenon (lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda, soap and the pH graph) and use all evidence from Lessons 1-9 and their revised particle model to write and present the Final Explanation. They compare their Lesson 1 model with the final model and close out the Driving Question Board.
slo.safetyNotes: No new practical chemicals are needed. If the pH graph is re-demonstrated with household products, never taste lab chemicals, wear goggles, wash hands after handling soap solution and keep lime and antacid samples away from the mouth and eyes. Emphasise that soap is harmful if swallowed and that antacids must be taken only as directed by a nurse or pharmacist.

LESSONS.overview: Mrs Achieng's class in Kisumu returns to the opening display: lemon juice from Kisumu market, vinegar, baking soda and bar soap, with the pH graph (lemon juice 2.0, vinegar 2.8, water 7.0, baking soda 8.3, soap 10.0). Learners first predict their final answer to the driving question, then review the evidence collected across the unit (indicator colours, H+ and OH- concentrations, reactions with metals and carbonates, neutralisation and stomach pH change, strong versus weak, and lime for Kericho soil). In the explain phase they write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning Final Explanation, applying it to a nurse or pharmacist in Nairobi giving magnesium hydroxide to a patient with hyperacidity after spicy nyama choma. They then complete the Driving Question Board by marking questions answered, compare their Lesson 1 model with the final particle model of H+ and OH- ions in each product, and present to peers.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look again at the pH graph and the four products from the Kisumu kitchen. Individually they write a 2-3 sentence prediction answering the driving question: 'Does the alkalinity of a substance determine its uses? Why are patients with hyperacidity given antacids?' They also rate their confidence from 1 to 3. Then they pair up (Think-Pair-Share) and compare answers, noting words they plan to use such as H+ (aq), OH- (aq), pH and neutralisation.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the pH graph and the four products. Say: 'Eight weeks ago Otieno asked why lemon is sour and Wanjiru asked why soap is slippery. Today you will answer the big question completely. Write your best answer now, using what you know.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before pairs start talking after the question is posed, then allow 3 minutes of writing. Cold-call 4 learners to share one idea from their partner (not their own). Record key words on the board without judging. Ask: 'What evidence would convince a sceptical neighbour that your answer is right?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share with confidence rating: surfacing prior ideas and confidence lets learners compare their starting point with their later, evidence-based answer, which builds metacognition and shows how their thinking has grown.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check written predictions: look for use of the terms acid, base, pH, neutralise; note learners who connect antacids to stomach acid versus those who only say 'it cures pain'. Observable indicator: at least 4 of 6 pairs mention both pH/ions and a use. Note confidence ratings for later comparison.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of four, learners complete an Evidence Gallery Walk with six stations made from their own notebooks and class charts: (1) pH graph data: lemon juice 2.0, vinegar 2.8, water 7.0, baking soda 8.3, soap 10.0 and the 10-fold H+ change per pH unit (lemon juice about 6 times more H+ than vinegar); (2) indicator colours: litmus, red cabbage and universal indicator; (3) H+ and OH- concentrations: lemon juice 1 x 10^-2 mol/L, vinegar about 1.6 x 10^-3 mol/L, soap OH- 1 x 10^-4 mol/L; (4) reactions: vinegar + baking soda fizzing with CO2 turning limewater milky, Mg + HCl giving H2 with a squeaky pop; (5) neutralisation and stomach pH: about 1.5 to 2 rising to about 3.5 to 5 after an antacid of magnesium hydroxide; (6) uses and strength: vinegar for pickling kachumbari, soap for cleaning, baking soda for Mama Wanjiru's mandazi, lime in Kericho raising soil pH from about 4.5 to 6.0 for maize, and HCl pH 1 versus ethanoic acid (acetic acid) pH 3. At each station they record one piece of evidence on an Evidence Card and note which lesson it came from.
framework.teacherMoves: Set a timer for 4 minutes per station. Circulate and ask: 'Which number on this chart best supports a use? Why that number?' and 'Is this about strength or about concentration?' At Station 6 prompt: 'Mr Kamau in Kericho adds lime. What is the lime doing to the H+ ions?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 3 groups to state the strongest piece of evidence they have found so far. Correct misconceptions promptly, for example that all bases are alkalis (only those that dissolve in water giving OH- (aq) are alkalis) or that a strong acid means a concentrated acid.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence Gallery Walk with Evidence Cards: collecting data from several sources into one set of cards lets learners see patterns across different kinds of evidence and prepares them to select the most relevant data for a claim.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each group has at least six Evidence Cards with correct values and the lesson source. Observable indicators: learners quote exact pH values, distinguish strength from concentration when questioned, and link at least one piece of evidence to each of the following: classification, ions, reactions, neutralisation, uses.

framework.learnerExperience: Individually, learners write their Final Explanation using the Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) frame. Claim: answers the driving question, that alkalinity, together with strength and safety, largely determines uses. Evidence: at least four data points, for example soap pH 10.0 and its slippery feel for cleaning, vinegar pH 2.8 for pickling, lime raising Kericho soil from about 4.5 to 6.0, and stomach pH rising from about 1.5 to 2 to about 3.5 to 5 after an antacid. Reasoning: link to ions, for example acids release H+ (aq), bases/alkalis neutralise acids or give OH- (aq), and H+ (aq) + OH- (aq) gives H2O, so acid + base gives salt + water. They must specifically explain why a patient in Nairobi with hyperacidity after eating spicy nyama choma is given magnesium hydroxide: excess stomach hydrochloric acid is neutralised, forming salt and water and raising stomach pH to a safer level. They also address the limits: strong bases such as sodium hydroxide (pH 13) are unsafe to swallow, which is why weak bases are chosen for antacids. Then in pairs they critique each other's CER using a checklist and revise.
framework.teacherMoves: Model one sentence stem only: 'I claim ___ because the data show ___, which means ___.' Say: 'Do not just state a fact. Tell me which number proves it and what the ions are doing.' Give 8 minutes of silent writing. Circulate and ask: 'Why is soap pH 10.0 good for cleaning but not for drinking?' and 'Why not give the patient sodium hydroxide at pH 13?' Allow WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Then run a peer critique: pairs swap and tick the checklist (claim, 4 data points with values, ion reasoning, antacid reaction, safety). Cold-call 5 learners to read one strong reasoning sentence aloud, and invite the class to say whether it uses evidence.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with peer critique: structuring the argument forces learners to connect data to a scientific principle, and peer critique exposes gaps so explanations become more complete and accurate.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use the CER checklist: (1) claim answers both parts of the driving question; (2) at least four correct values cited; (3) reasoning refers to H+ (aq) and OH- (aq) and neutralisation; (4) antacid explained as acid + base gives salt + water with stomach pH change; (5) mention of strength or safety. Observable indicator: at least 80% of learners meet 4 of 5 criteria; those below receive a targeted sentence-stem prompt.

framework.learnerExperience: The whole class revisits the Driving Question Board started in Lesson 1. Groups take the sticky notes, including Otieno's 'Why is lemon sour?' and Wanjiru's 'Why is soap slippery?', and sort them into 'Answered', 'Partly answered' and 'Still wondering'. For each answered question, a learner attaches the evidence card and the lesson number. Learners write one new question for future study, such as why bee stings or ant bites feel painful or how antacid tablets differ in strength, and add it to a 'Next Questions' area.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Walk to the board. Pick a question that you can now answer with evidence, not just opinion.' Allow WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before groups move. Ask 6 learners (cold-call) to read a question and state the evidence that answers it. Probe: 'Which lesson gave us that? What would we still need to test?' Highlight the unit's two key inquiry questions: how we classify acids and bases, and why they are important in daily life. Accept honest 'partly answered' notes, for example that learners have not yet measured exact stomach pH themselves.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board review: sorting questions by how well they have been answered makes the growth in understanding visible and gives learners ownership of the learning path, linking each question to specific evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether sorted questions are matched to correct evidence (for example, soap slipperiness to OH- (aq) from alkalis, sourness to H+ (aq)). Observable indicators: every group attaches at least two evidence cards with lesson numbers; at least one thoughtful new question is written per group.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out their Lesson 1 model (their first idea of why the four products differ) and draw their final particle model on a new page: four beakers (lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda solution, soap solution) showing H+ (aq) and OH- (aq) ions, with more H+ in lemon juice (pH 2.0) than vinegar (pH 2.8), more OH- in soap (pH 10.0) than baking soda (pH 8.3), and water at pH 7.0 as the neutral reference. They add a fifth drawing of the stomach with H+ (aq) and Cl- (aq) from hydrochloric acid, an antacid of magnesium hydroxide adding OH- (aq), and H+ + OH- forming H2O, with a pH arrow from about 1.5 to 2 up to about 3.5 to 5. Using a two-column table they compare 'Lesson 1 model' and 'Final model', listing what changed, and then present their final model to a partner and then to the class. They also fill in the summary table of what they observed, learned and explained.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Put your first model next to your new one. What have you added that you could not explain before?' Allow WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then 6 minutes for drawing. Check that ion numbers match the pH ordering (lemon juice < vinegar < water < baking soda < soap). Ask: 'Where do the H+ ions go when the antacid is swallowed?' and 'Why does the stomach pH rise but not reach 7?' Cold-call 4 learners to present one change between models. Use the Mama Wanjiru mandazi example to ask where the baking soda fits in the model. Remind learners that H3O+ is the form H+ takes in water, mentioned only as a note.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model comparison (before and after): placing the first and final models side by side makes conceptual change explicit, helping learners articulate how the particle-level explanation accounts for the phenomenon and its everyday uses.
framework.formativeAssessment: Rubric for the final model: (1) H+ and OH- ions correctly placed in each product; (2) relative amounts match the pH graph; (3) neutralisation in the stomach shown as H+ + OH- giving H2O; (4) pH arrow before and after the antacid; (5) at least two written changes from Lesson 1. Observable indicator: learners can explain, without notes, why the antacid helps a hyperacidity patient and why lime helps Kericho soil.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, review the CER write-ups and final models. Which learners still confuse strength with concentration, or treat all bases as alkalis? Did learners use specific pH values and ion reasoning rather than general statements? Did the antacid explanation include both the neutralisation reaction and the stomach pH change? Note which stations of the gallery walk prompted the best discussion and which evidence was ignored. Consider how participation differed across groups, whether any learners needed language support in writing, and what follow-up (for example, a short quiz or a home task interviewing a local pharmacist or farmer about antacids or lime) would consolidate learning.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that lemon juice (pH 2.0) and vinegar (pH 2.8) are acidic, sour and turn blue litmus red, while baking soda (pH 8.3) and soap (pH 10.0) are basic, bitter or slippery and turn red litmus blue. We also observed that acid + base reactions give salt + water, that stomach pH rises from about 1.5 to 2 to about 3.5 to 5 with an antacid, and that lime raises Kericho soil pH from about 4.5 to 6.0.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that acids release H+ (aq) ions and alkalis produce OH- (aq) ions, that lower pH means more H+, that strength (degree of ionisation) differs from concentration, and that properties such as pH, strength and safety determine how acids and bases are used for pickling, cleaning, baking, farming and medicine.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We explain that alkalinity, together with strength and safety, largely determines the uses of substances, and that patients with hyperacidity are given antacids such as magnesium hydroxide because the base neutralises excess stomach hydrochloric acid (H+ (aq) + OH- (aq) gives H2O, acid + base gives salt + water), raising the stomach pH to a safer level.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions:
In this Final Explanation you answer the driving question: Does the alkalinity of a substance determine its uses in day to day life? Why are patients with hyperacidity issues given antacid medications? Use the evidence you collected in Lessons 1 to 10 and your final particle model (H+ (aq) and OH- (aq) ions). Write in full sentences in the space under each prompt. In every answer, give a claim, evidence (use numbers and observations) and reasoning (use particles and ions). Use the pH data below. Refer to the Kisumu products, Mr Kamau in Kericho and the pharmacist in Nairobi where you can.

Data table (pH measured with a pH meter at 25 °C):

| Substance | pH |
|---|---|
| Lemon juice (Kisumu market) | 2.0 |
| Vinegar (5% ethanoic acid) | 2.8 |
| Pure water | 7.0 |
| Baking soda solution (as used for mandazi) | 8.3 |
| Bar soap solution | 10.0 |

sections.title: Part 1: Sorting products that look alike
sections.prompt: Lemon juice, vinegar, baking soda solution and soap solution look similar in clear cups, yet Otieno found lemon sour and Wanjiru found soap slippery. Using the pH table and the indicator results from your tests (litmus, red cabbage extract and universal indicator), classify each product as acid, base or neutral. Explain how the indicators and pH values agree even though the colours differ. Which product in each pair is more acidic or more basic: lemon juice and vinegar, soap and baking soda? Give the pH evidence.
sections.exemplar: Claim: Lemon juice and vinegar are acids, baking soda and soap are bases, and water is neutral. Evidence: Lemon juice (pH 2.0) and vinegar (pH 2.8) are below 7 and turn blue litmus red. Baking soda (pH 8.3) and soap (pH 10.0) are above 7 and turn red litmus blue. Water (pH 7.0) changes neither litmus paper. Red cabbage extract was red/pink in lemon juice, pink-red in vinegar, purple in water, blue-green in baking soda and green-yellow in soap. Universal indicator was red-orange (pH 2) in lemon juice, orange (pH 3) in vinegar, green (7) in water, blue (8) in baking soda and blue-purple (10) in soap. Reasoning: Different indicators have different colours, but each changes colour according to whether the substance is acidic, neutral or basic, so all give the same sorting. Universal indicator also shows how acidic or basic a substance is. Lemon juice (2.0) is more acidic than vinegar (2.8), a difference of 0.8 pH units. Soap (10.0) is more basic than baking soda (8.3), a difference of 1.7 pH units.

sections.title: Part 2: What is inside acids and alkalis?
sections.prompt: Explain at the particle level why lemon juice is sour and has a low pH, and why soap feels slippery. Use the Arrhenius definitions of an acid and an alkali, and the concentration data: lemon juice H+ = 1 x 10^-2 mol/L, vinegar H+ about 1.6 x 10^-3 mol/L, water 1 x 10^-7 mol/L, soap OH- = 1 x 10^-4 mol/L. Explain how much more H+ lemon juice has than vinegar, and say how you know. Describe how the Model you drew in Lesson 1 changed.
sections.exemplar: Claim: Lemon juice and vinegar are sour with low pH because they release H+ (aq) ions in water, and soap is slippery because it is an alkali that produces OH- (aq) ions. Evidence: Lemon juice has H+ of 1 x 10^-2 mol/L and vinegar about 1.6 x 10^-3 mol/L, far more than pure water at 1 x 10^-7 mol/L. Soap has OH- of 1 x 10^-4 mol/L, which is 1000 times more than water (1 x 10^-7 mol/L). Reasoning: An acid is a substance that produces H+ (aq) ions in water, so the citric acid in lemon juice and the ethanoic acid (acetic acid) in vinegar release H+ (aq). A lower pH means a higher H+ concentration, and each pH unit is a 10-fold change. Lemon juice is 0.8 pH units lower than vinegar, so it has about 6 times more H+ (10^0.8 is about 6.3), which is why it is more sour. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water and produces OH- (aq) ions; these ions react with the oils on the skin, giving the slippery feel. Baking soda gives fewer OH- ions than soap, so it is only weakly basic (pH 8.3). My Lesson 1 model had only a guess that something differed inside the products; my final model shows more H+ (aq) in lemon juice and vinegar and more OH- (aq) in baking soda and soap.

sections.title: Part 3: How acids and bases behave
sections.prompt: When vinegar was added to baking soda it fizzed. Magnesium ribbon was placed in dilute hydrochloric acid. Describe what you observed and how you tested each gas. Explain why these reactions happen with acids but not with soap or water, and write word equations for the two reactions. Then explain what happens, in terms of ions, when an acid and a base are mixed.
sections.exemplar: Claim: Acids react with carbonates and reactive metals because of their H+ (aq) ions, and acids and bases react together in neutralisation. Evidence: Vinegar and lemon juice fizzed with baking soda, and the gas turned limewater milky, showing carbon dioxide; water with baking soda did not fizz. Magnesium in dilute hydrochloric acid gave bubbles and the gas burned with a squeaky pop (lighted splint), showing hydrogen; magnesium in water gave no bubbles. Reasoning: The H+ (aq) ions in acids react with the carbonate-type baking soda and with magnesium. Acid + carbonate gives salt + water + carbon dioxide. Acid + metal gives salt + hydrogen. Soap and water do not release H+ (aq) so they do not do this. In neutralisation, acid + base gives salt + water; in terms of ions, H+ (aq) + OH- (aq) gives H2O (l). In the investigation, universal indicator moved from red towards orange, yellow and green as magnesium hydroxide or baking soda was added to dilute hydrochloric acid, showing that the pH rose.

sections.title: Part 4: Strength, safety and uses
sections.prompt: Otieno asked: if both are acids, why is lemon juice lower on the graph than vinegar? Use the data for 0.1 M hydrochloric acid (pH 1), 0.1 M ethanoic acid (pH 3), 0.1 M sodium hydroxide (pH 13) and 0.1 M ammonia solution (pH 11) to explain the difference between strength and concentration. Then explain why a weak base such as magnesium hydroxide is a safer antacid than a strong base, and why soap is useful for cleaning but harmful if swallowed.
sections.exemplar: Claim: Strength depends on how much an acid or base ionises, not on how much is dissolved, and strength affects safety and uses. Evidence: At the same concentration of 0.1 M, hydrochloric acid has pH 1 but ethanoic acid has pH 3, and sodium hydroxide has pH 13 but ammonia has pH 11. Reasoning: Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide are strong because they ionise almost completely, giving many H+ (aq) or OH- (aq) ions. Ethanoic acid and ammonia are weak because they ionise only partly, giving fewer ions even though the same amount is dissolved. Concentration is how much is dissolved; strength is how much ionises. A strong base would add a lot of OH- (aq) and could be harmful in the body, so a weak base such as magnesium hydroxide is a safer antacid. Soap (pH 10.0) has OH- (aq) that helps remove grease, which makes it useful for cleaning, but the same alkalinity is harmful if swallowed, so it needs safety precautions. In the laboratory we never taste chemicals and we wear goggles.

sections.title: Part 5: Answering the driving question
sections.prompt: Write your final Claim-Evidence-Reasoning answer to the driving question: Does the alkalinity of a substance determine its uses in day to day life? Why are patients with hyperacidity issues given antacid medications? Use at least three uses (for example vinegar, soap, baking soda, Mr Kamau's lime in Kericho, the pharmacist in Nairobi). Include the stomach pH values and the soil pH values. Say what else, besides alkalinity, matters.
sections.exemplar: Claim: Yes, alkalinity largely determines uses, together with strength and safety. Patients with hyperacidity are given antacids because the base in the antacid neutralises excess stomach hydrochloric acid. Evidence: Vinegar (pH 2.8) is an acid used by mama mboga for pickling kachumbari and onions. Soap (pH 10.0) is an alkali used for cleaning grease. Baking soda (pH 8.3) is weakly basic and safe in small amounts in mandazi. In Kericho, Mr Kamau uses lime to raise acidic soil from pH about 4.5 to about 6.0 for maize. After eating spicy nyama choma in Nairobi, a patient with hyperacidity is given magnesium hydroxide, which raises stomach pH from about 1.5 to 2 to about 3.5 to 5. Reasoning: Bases neutralise acids: acid + base gives salt + water, and H+ (aq) + OH- (aq) gives H2O (l). The OH- (aq) from lime reacts with H+ (aq) in the soil, and the base in the antacid reacts with H+ (aq) from stomach hydrochloric acid, raising the pH to a safer level. Acids are useful for preservation and flavour, and bases for cleaning, baking and neutralising acids. Strength and safety also matter: a weak base such as magnesium hydroxide is chosen as an antacid because it is safer than a strong base, and soap is useful but harmful if swallowed.

rubric.excellent: Gives a clear claim that alkalinity, with strength and safety, largely determines uses, and states why antacids are given for hyperacidity.
rubric.proficient: Gives a claim about uses and antacids but leaves out strength or safety.
rubric.developing: Claim is missing, unclear or does not address both parts of the question.

rubric.excellent: Uses exact pH values, concentrations, indicator colours, reaction tests and stomach/soil pH changes correctly in every part.
rubric.proficient: Uses most data correctly, with one or two missing or small errors.
rubric.developing: Uses little data, or data is incorrect or not linked to the claim.

rubric.excellent: Explains using H+ (aq) and OH- (aq), the Arrhenius definitions, the 10-fold pH change and H+ (aq) + OH- (aq) gives H2O (l) accurately.
rubric.proficient: Mentions H+ and OH- ions correctly but explanations are incomplete.
rubric.developing: Does not use ions, or confuses acids and bases.

rubric.excellent: Clearly separates strength from concentration using the HCl, ethanoic acid, NaOH and ammonia data, and links this to safe antacid and soap use.
rubric.proficient: Describes strength correctly but does not link to safety clearly.
rubric.developing: Confuses strength with concentration or omits safety.

rubric.excellent: Links to Kisumu products, Kericho lime and the Nairobi pharmacist; uses correct terms in clear, organised sentences.
rubric.proficient: Uses some contexts and mostly correct terms.
rubric.developing: Little context; terms are misused or writing is hard to follow.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: Does the alkalinity of a substance determine its uses in day to day life? Why are patients with hyperacidity issues given antacid medications?

lessons.title: Phenomenon: Why Do Lemon Juice, Vinegar, Baking Soda and Soap Behave So Differently?
lessons.observed: We observed that lemon juice (pH 2.0) and vinegar (pH 2.8) have pH values below pure water (pH 7.0), while baking soda solution (pH 8.3) and soap solution (pH 10.0) are above 7. Lemon juice and vinegar taste sour and are safe in food, baking soda tastes bitter/salty and is safe in small amounts in food, and soap feels slippery and is harmful if swallowed.
lessons.learned: We learned that products that look alike can be on different sides of 7 on the pH scale, and that their uses (vinegar for pickling, soap for cleaning, baking soda for mandazi, lemon juice for flavour and tea) seem to match their pH, taste and feel.
lessons.explained: We can so far hypothesise that something different inside lemon juice and vinegar from inside baking soda and soap causes the difference in pH, taste and feel, and that antacids may help hyperacidity because they are on the other side of the scale from stomach acid. We still need evidence to test this idea.

lessons.title: Sorting the Kitchen: Classifying Household Substances as Acids or Bases with Litmus and Red Cabbage
lessons.observed: Record what you saw: the colour of red litmus, blue litmus and red cabbage extract in lemon juice, vinegar, water, baking soda solution and soap solution.
lessons.learned: Write how you can sort a substance as an acid or a base using the pattern of colour changes: acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue; water does not change either.
lessons.explained: Explain how the indicator results classify the four kitchen products, how they compare with your Lesson 1 hypotheses and pH values (2.0, 2.8, 7.0, 8.3, 10.0), and what you still want to find out about why they behave this way and how this might affect their uses.

lessons.title: Natural and Laboratory Indicators: Building a Classification Table
lessons.observed: We tested lemon juice, vinegar, water, baking soda solution and soap solution with red cabbage extract and universal indicator. Red cabbage: lemon juice red/pink, vinegar pink-red, water purple, baking soda blue-green, soap green-yellow. Universal indicator: lemon juice red-orange (pH 2), vinegar orange (pH 3), water green (7), baking soda blue (8), soap blue-purple (10).
lessons.learned: Indicators show whether a substance is acidic, neutral or basic. Natural indicators such as red cabbage extract and laboratory indicators such as litmus and universal indicator all give the same sorting, even though the colours differ. Universal indicator also shows how acidic or basic a substance is on the pH scale. Water is neutral (pH 7.0).
lessons.explained: Lemon juice (pH 2.0) and vinegar (pH 2.8) are acids; baking soda (pH 8.3) and soap (pH 10.0) are bases; water (pH 7.0) is neutral. Lemon juice is more acidic than vinegar, and soap is more basic than baking soda. Our hypotheses from Lesson 1 are supported by the indicator evidence and the pH values, and our model shows more H+ in the acids and more OH- in the bases. We still need to explain why acids are sour and soap is slippery.

lessons.title: Why is Lemon Juice Sour? Acids Release H⁺ Ions in Water (Arrhenius Definition)
lessons.observed: We observed that lemon juice (pH 2.0, H+ = 1 x 10^-2 mol/L) and vinegar (pH 2.8, H+ about 1.6 x 10^-3 mol/L) have much more H+ than pure water (pH 7.0, H+ = 1 x 10^-7 mol/L), and in the simulation the acid molecules released H+ (aq) ions when they dissolved in water. Lemon juice has about 6 times more H+ than vinegar.
lessons.learned: We learned that an acid is a substance that produces H+ (aq) ions in water (Arrhenius definition), and that a lower pH means a higher H+ concentration. Each pH unit is a 10-fold change in H+ concentration.
lessons.explained: We can explain that lemon juice and vinegar are sour, turn blue litmus red and have low pH because the acids (citric acid and ethanoic acid (acetic acid)) release H+ (aq) ions in water; lemon juice is more sour than vinegar because it has about 6 times more H+. Stomach acid is also an acid with H+ ions, which helps us start to understand why antacids are needed; we still need to learn what particles bases like baking soda and soap release.

lessons.title: Arrhenius Definition (Bases and Alkalis): Why Does Soap Feel Slippery?
lessons.observed: Red litmus turned blue in baking soda solution and soap solution, but stayed red in lemon juice and vinegar. Soap solution (pH 10.0) felt slippery, baking soda solution (pH 8.3) was only weakly basic, and soap has an OH- concentration of 1 x 10^-4 mol/L, 1000 times more than pure water (1 x 10^-7 mol/L).
lessons.learned: Bases that dissolve in water are called alkalis and they produce OH- (aq) ions (Arrhenius definition). All alkalis are bases but not all bases dissolve in water. Soap has more OH- ions than baking soda, so it has a higher pH.
lessons.explained: Soap feels slippery because it is an alkali that releases OH- (aq) ions in water, and these ions react with the oils on the skin. Baking soda gives fewer OH- ions, so it is only weakly basic and safe in small amounts in mandazi. Our particle model now shows H+ (aq) in lemon juice and vinegar and OH- (aq) in baking soda and soap.

lessons.title: Chemical Properties I: How Acids React with Metals and Carbonates
lessons.observed: Vinegar mixed with baking soda fizzed, and the gas turned limewater milky. Lemon juice also fizzed with baking soda, but water with baking soda did not. Magnesium ribbon in dilute hydrochloric acid gave bubbles, and the gas burned with a squeaky pop. Magnesium in water showed no bubbles.
lessons.learned: Acids react with reactive metals such as magnesium to give a salt and hydrogen gas, and with carbonates such as baking soda to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide. Hydrogen is tested with a lighted splint (squeaky pop) and carbon dioxide with limewater (turns milky). These reactions happen because of the H+ (aq) ions in acids.
lessons.explained: The fizzing in the Kisumu kitchen happens because vinegar and lemon juice are acids that release H+ (aq) ions, which react with the carbonate-type baking soda to give carbon dioxide. Soap does not do this because it is a base. This shows that the acidic or basic nature of a substance decides how it behaves and is used, which helps us answer the driving question and prepares us to explain how antacids deal with hyperacidity.

lessons.title: Chemical Properties II: Neutralisation and Antacids
lessons.observed: When magnesium hydroxide (or baking soda) was added to dilute hydrochloric acid with universal indicator, the colour changed from red towards orange, yellow and green as the pH rose; adding water alone changed it very little. The stomach pH rises from about 1.5 to 2 to about 3.5 to 5 after an antacid.
lessons.learned: Neutralisation is a reaction between an acid and a base that gives salt + water. In terms of ions, H+ (aq) + OH- (aq) gives H2O (l). Antacids contain bases such as magnesium hydroxide or calcium carbonate.
lessons.explained: Patients with hyperacidity are given antacids because the base neutralises some of the excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach, forming salt and water and raising the pH to a safer level, so the use of a base as medicine depends on its alkalinity (and, as we will see, on its strength and safety).

lessons.title: Strength of Acids and Bases and the pH Scale
lessons.observed: With universal indicator, 0.1 M hydrochloric acid showed pH 1 and 0.1 M ethanoic acid showed pH 3; 0.1 M sodium hydroxide showed pH 13 and 0.1 M ammonia showed pH 11. Lemon juice (pH 2.0) is lower than vinegar (pH 2.8) on the pH graph.
lessons.learned: Strength is about the degree of ionisation, not concentration. A strong acid or base ionises almost completely, while a weak one ionises only partly. Each pH unit is a 10-fold change in H+ concentration, so lemon juice has about 6 times more H+ (aq) than vinegar.
lessons.explained: At equal concentration, HCl gives many more H+ (aq) ions than ethanoic acid, so its pH is lower; NaOH gives more OH- (aq) than ammonia, so its pH is higher. This helps explain why a weak base like magnesium hydroxide is a safer antacid for hyperacidity than a strong base, and it advances our answer that alkalinity, together with strength and safety, influences how products are used.

lessons.title: Uses of Acids and Bases and Safety: Why Vinegar Pickles, Soap Cleans, Lime Heals Soil and Antacids Soothe
lessons.observed: Vinegar (pH 2.8) is used by mama mboga to pickle kachumbari and onions; soap solution (pH 10.0) lifts grease; baking soda (pH 8.3) is used for mandazi; lime raises Kericho soil from pH about 4.5 to about 6.0 for maize; a magnesium hydroxide antacid raises stomach pH from about 1.5-2 to about 3.5-5 after spicy nyama choma.
lessons.learned: The uses of acids and bases depend on their nature (H+ (aq) or OH- (aq)), their pH and their strength, and each use needs matching safety precautions: acids help preserve and flavour food, bases clean, bake and neutralise acids in soil and in the stomach, and not every acid or base is safe in the same way.
lessons.explained: Alkalinity largely determines uses because bases neutralise acids (acid + base gives salt + water): lime neutralises H+ (aq) in acidic soil, antacids neutralise excess hydrochloric acid in hyperacidity, and soap's OH- (aq) helps remove grease, while strength and safety decide how they can be used.

lessons.title: Consolidation: Answering the Driving Question – Alkalinity, Uses and Antacids
lessons.observed: We observed that lemon juice (pH 2.0) and vinegar (pH 2.8) are acidic, sour and turn blue litmus red, while baking soda (pH 8.3) and soap (pH 10.0) are basic, bitter or slippery and turn red litmus blue. We also observed that acid + base reactions give salt + water, that stomach pH rises from about 1.5 to 2 to about 3.5 to 5 with an antacid, and that lime raises Kericho soil pH from about 4.5 to 6.0.
lessons.learned: We learned that acids release H+ (aq) ions and alkalis produce OH- (aq) ions, that lower pH means more H+, that strength (degree of ionisation) differs from concentration, and that properties such as pH, strength and safety determine how acids and bases are used for pickling, cleaning, baking, farming and medicine.
lessons.explained: We explain that alkalinity, together with strength and safety, largely determines the uses of substances, and that patients with hyperacidity are given antacids such as magnesium hydroxide because the base neutralises excess stomach hydrochloric acid (H+ (aq) + OH- (aq) gives H2O, acid + base gives salt + water), raising the stomach pH to a safer level.
